EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong shortwave trough aided in the development of scattered to numerous thunderstorms during the late morning, afternoon, and evening hours of March 21. Thunderstorms initially fired along a dryline, many of which became severe, and some of which produced strong tornadoes. A total of 17 tornadoes were confirmed by storm survey teams, the strongest of which was the EF-3 Jacksboro tornado. One death occurred in a tornado in Grayson County near the Red River.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The tornado began on the south side of Bowie along State Highway 101 where damage was found to multiple single family residences including one home that shifted off the foundation causing the walls and roof to collapse caused by wind speeds estimated between 105 to 110 mph. There were 3 injuries reported with damage in this area. As the tornado moved north-northeast along the eastern side of Bowie, many structures spanning from FM 3043 to just south of State Highway 59 and Haney Rd were damaged including several single family and manufactured homes where the roofs and walls were lifted and destroyed in places. Just before the tornado lifted, a manufactured home was destroyed with damage spanning 1/4 mile by this point in the path. Maximum estimated winds were 110 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A stationary front extended from west to east along the I-20 corridor of East Texas and North Louisiana around daybreak on April 17th, which slowly lifted back north into Northeast Texas and Southern Arkansas through the afternoon. Meanwhile, an upper level trough dove southeast through the Southern Plains during the day, reinforcing a cold front southeast across the region. These features enhanced large scale ascent as they interacted with a warm, moist, and unstable air mass that had begun to surge back to the north. As a result, scattered showers and thunderstorms developed and spread east-northeast from late morning through the afternoon across Northeast Texas, Southwest Arkansas, and North Louisiana. An isolated severe thunderstorm developed over Titus County Texas, producing large hail near the Winfield community before shifting off to the east into Southwest Arkansas and North Louisiana through the afternoon.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Ping pong ball size hail fell just northeast of the Winfield community on Highway 67.

A potent upper level low pressure system over New Mexico shifted east across Western and North Texas south of the Red River during the afternoon and evening hours of October 24th, which allowed for a dry line to mix east across Texas. A cold front extended east of this upper low over Eastern Oklahoma and Northeast Texas, with the dry line eventually overtaking the front but provided strong forcing for a linear line of showers and thunderstorms to develop during the evening and overnight hours as they entered East Texas. Although instability was limited given cooler conditions during the latter evening hours, strong shear resulted in a well-organized line of strong to severe thunderstorms along these surface features, producing damaging winds which downed trees across portions of East Texas before the storms weakened further upon entering Western Louisiana during the early morning hours on the 25th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple trees were blown down on Highway 315 several miles northeast of Mount Enterprise.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A shortwave trough moved through the upper pattern and pushed a cold front through South Central Texas. Thunderstorms developed along this front and produced damaging wind gusts and one tornado.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A National Weather Service storm survey team determined a tornado touched down just west of CR 234 and north of CR 239. The tornado moved southeastward producing EF-0 damage to trees and a barn and knocked down a two-story home that was still under construction near CR 310 and CR 237. As the tornado crossed this intersection it turned east and strengthened and widened. High end EF-0 damage was observed to trees and some homes just to the west of I-35. The tornado crossed I-35 south of CR 314 and north of Ronald Reagan Blvd. and strengthened further. A semi-trailer was flipped on I-35 and the driver sustained minor injuries. Nine wooden power poles were brought down on the north bound side of I-35, including one that was snapped in half. As the tornado continued east of I-35 and west of Little Road EF-1 damage was observed. Additional power poles were damaged and snapped. A home sustained roof damage and many large tree branches were snapped. A barn had a portion of the roof removed. A small, enclosed cargo trailer on the property was lofted roughly 100 yards downwind. Maximum winds were estimated at 100 mph just east of I-35. The tornado dissipated east of Little Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Very strong rip currents at local beaches on the afternoon of October 12th contributed to a drowning on South Padre Island.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A 17-year old man drowned in a rip current at approximately 4 PM CDT on Wednesday, October 12th, in the surf at Cameron County Public Access #5. The teen was with a group of peers but entered the surf on his own and, according to the witnesses, disappeared into the waves. According to USCG, witnesses reported the swimmer began demonstrating signs of distress, and the currents soon overpowered him before he submerged. A 9-1-1 call from the peer group was related to USCG Corpus Christi, where air assets were deployed, along with water assets from USCG South Padre Island to assist with SAR. Cameron County Beach Patrol, Cameron County Emergency Management, and South Padre island Fire Department assisted in the SAR. The swimmer was recovered a day later (October 13), 8 miles north of the entry point, by Cameron Co. Park Rangers after fishers discovered the floating body and called 9-1-1.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A compact but strong upper level low pressure system dropped southeast across New Mexico on the 27th. Cold temperatures aloft and abundant low level moisture were able to create a modestly unstable environment within an atmosphere of strong wind shear. The combination of these features created strong thunderstorms on the afternoon and evening of the 27th. One of these storms produced ping ping ball size hail as it moved over Cee Vee (Cottle County). Lingering moderate rain showers early in the morning of the 28th generated a brief period of severe wind gusts near Brownfield (Terry County). A Texas Texas University West Texas mesonet site near Brownfield measured severe wind gusts from 0603 CST through 0607 CST with a peak gust of 65 mph.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Local broadcast media relayed a photograph of hail up to ping pong ball size.

Several heavy rain episodes during August led to above normal precipitation across South Central Texas. Much of the western half of the area received three to four times their normal. The result was improvement on the drought in all but two counties. The central part of the area had the least rain and Comal County was the only county that saw the drought worsen from Extreme (D3) category to Exceptional (D4) category. Next door Hays County remained in D3. All other counties saw improvement. Bandera, Gillespie, Gonzales, Kerr, Kinney, Maverick, Real, Uvalde, and Wilson improved from D4 to Severe (D2) category. Bexar, Blanco, Guadalupe, Kendall, and Medina improved from D4 to D3. Burnet, Caldwell, Llano, and Williamson improved from D3 to D2. Of the counties in D2 or worse drought Maverick, Kerr, Bandera, Medina, Bexar, Comal, Hays, and Wilson had outdoor burn bans in effect at the end of the month. The 7-day average streamflow on the Nueces River was normal (25%-75%), the Frio River was much below normal (<10%), the Medina River was below normal (10%-24%), the San Antonio River was normal, the upper Guadalupe River was much below normal, the lower Guadalupe River was below normal, the upper Colorado River was normal to below normal and the lower Colorado River was below to much below (<10%) normal. The Edwards Aquifer rose 4.2 feet, but was still 27.2 feet below normal. Lake Amistad rose 9.8 feet, but was still 54.1 feet below normal conservation pool level. Medina Lake dropped 4.2 feet and was 75.7 feet below normal and Lake Travis fell 1.7 feet to 36.2 feet below normal. Most public water systems encouraged at least voluntary water restrictions and many had mandatory restrictions in effect. Some of the larger services had the following: Fredericksburg Stage 3, New Braunfels Stage 1, San Antonio Stage 2, San Marcos Stage 2, Austin Stage 1, Kerrville Stage 1, and Georgetown Stage 2.

Extreme drought (D3) conditions expanded during the month of January due to continued drier than normal conditions. Most of the expansion of D3 was observed in the Rolling Plains which now includes Hall, King, Dickens, Crosby, and Stonewall Counties. Moderate (D1) to Severe (D2) drought conditions expanded elsewhere across the remainder of the region.||These drought conditions were strongly tied to a mature moderate strength La Ni��a over the tropical eastern Pacific Ocean. Several drier than average months have led to these conditions. The latest three month precipitation amounts continued to range from 5% to 25% of normal. The only beneficial rainfall fell around New Year's Day but was too little to cause an improvement in long term drought conditions. After record breaking temperatures in December, January saw several but brief cold spells which brought monthly temperatures slightly below seasonal normals. There are few agricultural impacts this time of year with most of the area cotton already harvested. However, winter wheat emergence has been very poor to this date. Furthermore, livestock was being fed supplemental feed due to poor native grasslands.

On the morning of New Year's Day, the strongest cold front of the season to date moved through the region bringing falling temperatures throughout the day. During the evening, a short wave trough swung out of the southern Rockies and across the Southern Plains. Lift from this short wave acted upon the moisture and cold air in place over the region creating widespread light snowfall. Snow began late in the afternoon and only lasted until early in the evening. Most areas saw one inch or less of snow accumulation but a few locations did see higher amounts. Areas across the city of Lubbock (Lubbock County) saw snowfall amounts generally ranging from one inch to three inches. An intensifying storm system dropping through the center of the nation brought a prolonged period of wind to West Texas from the afternoon of the 14th into the morning of the 15th. A strong cold front moved through during the afternoon and evening hours, switching the winds around to the north and carrying much colder air on strong winds. Blowing dust peaked on the evening of the 14th, along and behind the frontal passage, while temperatures tumbled into the 20s by early on the 15th. Stout northerly winds continued to blow Friday night and through much of Saturday, generally peaking during the overnight hours, before finally diminishing Saturday evening as the storm system shifted off to the east. Peak wind gusts of 58 to 66 mph were common, favoring the southeast Texas Panhandle and Rolling Plains. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong cold front and compact upper level storm system joined forces to bring a brief bout of wintry weather in late January. The initial cold front moved through the region on the evening of the 25th, complete with gusty easterly winds and temperatures tumbling from the upper 40s and 50s into the lower to middle 20s by early the next morning. Clouds gradually filled in behind the front and light precipitation developed early on the 26th. Farther south, where moisture and lift were shallower, areas of light freezing drizzle affected much of the South Plains. The freezing drizzle switched to snow in spots, as stronger lift from the approaching system spread over the region. One intense band of snow formed over the central South Plains, just north of Lubbock, and advanced northeastward across Floydada, Flomot, Memphis, and Childress during the afternoon. Where the snow band lingered longest, many locations recorded one to three inches of snow, while Estelline measured 4.3 inches. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong southwesterly low level jet, which developed ahead of an area of low pressure along a cold front over Southern Oklahoma, quickly resulted in the transport of low level moisture north-northeast into East Texas, Southwest Arkansas, and North Louisiana, ahead of a shortwave trough that traversed the Red River Valley into Southern Arkansas and North Louisiana during the afternoon of January 19th. This cold front was reinforced south into Northeast Texas and Southwest Arkansas during the afternoon, with breaks in the cloud cover ahead of the front resulting in some destabilization near the surface. Mid level lapse rates steepened in the expanding warm sector ahead of the approaching shortwave trough, with increased large scale forcing resulting in expanding coverage of showers and thunderstorms. Some of these storms became severe across portions of East Texas, with reports of large hail over Gregg and Harrison Counties. Hail as large as tennis balls fell across portions of Marshall in Harrison County, before the storms weakened considerably as they entered extreme Northwest Louisiana during the late afternoon and early evening.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hen egg size hail fell in Marshall.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A potent upper level low pressure system over New Mexico shifted east across Western and North Texas south of the Red River during the afternoon and evening hours of October 24th, which allowed for a dry line to mix east across Texas. A cold front extended east of this upper low over Eastern Oklahoma and Northeast Texas, with the dry line eventually overtaking the front but provided strong forcing for a linear line of showers and thunderstorms to develop during the evening and overnight hours as they entered East Texas. Although instability was limited given cooler conditions during the latter evening hours, strong shear resulted in a well-organized line of strong to severe thunderstorms along these surface features, producing damaging winds which downed trees across portions of East Texas before the storms weakened further upon entering Western Louisiana during the early morning hours on the 25th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was blown down on the westbound lane on Highway 204 at the Cherokee/Nacogdoches County line near the Sacul community.

A strong southwesterly low level jet, which developed ahead of an area of low pressure along a cold front over Southern Oklahoma, quickly resulted in the transport of low level moisture north-northeast into East Texas, Southwest Arkansas, and North Louisiana, ahead of a shortwave trough that traversed the Red River Valley into Southern Arkansas and North Louisiana during the afternoon of January 19th. This cold front was reinforced south into Northeast Texas and Southwest Arkansas during the afternoon, with breaks in the cloud cover ahead of the front resulting in some destabilization near the surface. Mid level lapse rates steepened in the expanding warm sector ahead of the approaching shortwave trough, with increased large scale forcing resulting in expanding coverage of showers and thunderstorms. Some of these storms became severe across portions of East Texas, with reports of large hail over Gregg and Harrison Counties. Rainfall was a bit of a mixed bag in October. A swath of the central part of the area had 10-50% of normal. The area along the Rio Grande had 100-200% of normal. The rest of the area was in between. There was enough rainfall in Bandera County for that county to improve from Extreme (D3) drought to Severe (D2) drought. Lack of rain worsened the drought from D2 to D3 in Fayette and Gonzales Counties. All other counties remained where they were in September. Comal, Guadalupe, and Hays stayed in Exceptional (D4) drought. Bexar, Blanco, Caldwell, Kendall, and Medina remained in D3. Bastrop, Burnet, Gillespie, Kerr, Kinney, Lavaca, Llano, Real, Travis, Uvalde, Williamson, and Wilson stayed in D2. Of the counties in D2 or worse drought Comal, Guadalupe, Hays, Bexar, Blanco, Caldwell, Fayette, Gonzales, Kendall, Medina, Burnet, Gillespie, Llano, Travis, and Wilson had outdoor burn bans in effect at the end of the month. The 7-day average streamflow at the end of the month was normal (25%-75%) to below normal (10%-24%) on the Nueces River, much below normal (<10%) on the Frio River, below normal (10%-24%) on the Medina River, below normal (10%-24%) on the San Antonio River, much below normal (<10%) on the upper and lower Guadalupe River, and normal (25%-75%) to below normal (10%-24%) on the upper Colorado River. Area reservoirs were below normal pool level. Lake Amistad rose 4.5 feet, but was still 37.0 feel below normal. Medina Lake decreased 1.2 feet to 78.0 feet below normal and Lake Travis dropped 2.4 feet to 40.6 feet below normal. The Edwards Aquifer rose 2.3 feet, but was 33.2 feet below average. Most public water systems encouraged at least voluntary water restrictions and many had mandatory restrictions in effect. Some of the larger services had the following: New Braunfels Stage 1, San Antonio Stage 2, Austin Stage 1, and Kerrville Stage 1.

Extreme drought (D3) conditions expanded during the month of January due to continued drier than normal conditions. Most of the expansion of D3 was observed in the Rolling Plains which now includes Hall, King, Dickens, Crosby, and Stonewall Counties. Moderate (D1) to Severe (D2) drought conditions expanded elsewhere across the remainder of the region.||These drought conditions were strongly tied to a mature moderate strength La Ni��a over the tropical eastern Pacific Ocean. Rainfall was a bit of a mixed bag in October. A swath of the central part of the area had 10-50% of normal. The area along the Rio Grande had 100-200% of normal. The rest of the area was in between. There was enough rainfall in Bandera County for that county to improve from Extreme (D3) drought to Severe (D2) drought. Lack of rain worsened the drought from D2 to D3 in Fayette and Gonzales Counties. All other counties remained where they were in September. Comal, Guadalupe, and Hays stayed in Exceptional (D4) drought. Bexar, Blanco, Caldwell, Kendall, and Medina remained in D3. Bastrop, Burnet, Gillespie, Kerr, Kinney, Lavaca, Llano, Real, Travis, Uvalde, Williamson, and Wilson stayed in D2. Of the counties in D2 or worse drought Comal, Guadalupe, Hays, Bexar, Blanco, Caldwell, Fayette, Gonzales, Kendall, Medina, Burnet, Gillespie, Llano, Travis, and Wilson had outdoor burn bans in effect at the end of the month. The 7-day average streamflow at the end of the month was normal (25%-75%) to below normal (10%-24%) on the Nueces River, much below normal (<10%) on the Frio River, below normal (10%-24%) on the Medina River, below normal (10%-24%) on the San Antonio River, much below normal (<10%) on the upper and lower Guadalupe River, and normal (25%-75%) to below normal (10%-24%) on the upper Colorado River. Area reservoirs were below normal pool level. Lake Amistad rose 4.5 feet, but was still 37.0 feel below normal. Medina Lake decreased 1.2 feet to 78.0 feet below normal and Lake Travis dropped 2.4 feet to 40.6 feet below normal. The Edwards Aquifer rose 2.3 feet, but was 33.2 feet below average. Most public water systems encouraged at least voluntary water restrictions and many had mandatory restrictions in effect. Some of the larger services had the following: New Braunfels Stage 1, San Antonio Stage 2, Austin Stage 1, and Kerrville Stage 1.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the morning of New Year's Day, the strongest cold front of the season to date moved through the region bringing falling temperatures throughout the day. During the evening, a short wave trough swung out of the southern Rockies and across the Southern Plains. Lift from this short wave acted upon the moisture and cold air in place over the region creating widespread light snowfall. Snow began late in the afternoon and only lasted until early in the evening. Most areas saw one inch or less of snow accumulation but a few locations did see higher amounts. Areas across the city of Lubbock (Lubbock County) saw snowfall amounts generally ranging from one inch to three inches. NWS cooperative weather observers in Plainview (Hale County) and Matador (Motley County) measured 2.0 inches of snowfall.||Additionally, virga showers during the early morning hours brought isolated severe wind gusts due to very dry surface air at the time.||The Texas Tech University West Texas mesonet sites below measured severe wind gusts:||67 mph at Levelland (Hockley County),|64 mph at Denver City (Yoakum County), and|58 mph at Caprock Canyons State Park (Briscoe County).

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe (D2) to Extreme (D3) drought conditions returned across Red River County, Texas in early October, and lingered throughout the remainder of the month. This was in response to an extended flash drought that resulted from an exceptionally hot and dry month in June with below normal rainfall in what is historically one of the wettest months on average. This was followed up by an even hotter and drier month in July with the total rainfall amounts for July generally around an inch or less, which was only near 25% of normal. Near normal rainfall occurred in August, but hot and dry conditions returned in September with below normal rainfall while October rainfall was near normal. This dryness contributed to lower than normal streamflow observed across area creeks, streams, and rivers.

Some beneficial rainfall occurred over portions of the Brush Country and Coastal Bend during the last week of the month. Drought conditions improved over these regions. But most of south Texas received well below normal rainfall with drought conditions worsening over the northern Coastal Bend and western Victoria Crossroads.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Extreme to severe drought over the county improved to just severe drought over the western half of the county by the end of the month.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms produced localized flash flooding in Crockett County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Law enforcement reported 3 feet of water on the road, which resulted in two cars stalling out. Also, law enforcement reported a semi-trailer truck had water up to the radiator.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered thunderstorms produced a few severe weather reports during the afternoon across the Big Country and Heartland.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Also, there were reported wind gusts between 40 and 58 mph in Rule.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Most of the western half of South Central Texas received less than 25% of normal precipitation during January and the north central part of the area had less than 75% of normal. The lack of rainfall led to Severe (D2) Drought conditions developing in Atascosa, Bandera, Blanco, Burnet, Frio, Gillespie, Kendall, Kerr, Kinney, Llano, Medina, Real, Uvalde, and Zavala Counties. Dimmit County worsened from Severe to Extreme (D3) and Edwards, Maverick, and Val Verde remained in D2. At the end of the month, the seven day streamflow for rivers in the region were below to much below normal. The Edwards Aquifer was 4.6 feet below normal. Area reservoirs were below normal. Lake Amistad was 48 feet below normal and Medina Lake was 47.3 feet below normal. Of the counties in D2 or worse drought Atascosa, Blanco, Burnet, Dimmit, Frio, Kendall, Kinney, Llano, Maverick, Val Verde, and Zavala had outdoor burn bans in effect.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An approaching short wave aloft along with increasing low level moisture allowed scattered thunderstorms to develop on the afternoon into the evening of the 16th across eastern New Mexico. This activity developed eastward, organizing into a ragged line of high based thunderstorms as it moved across the South Plains, then into the Rolling Plains during the evening and overnight hours. These thunderstorms produced widespread strong to severe winds as they accelerated eastward, along with blowing dust.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A Texas Tech University West Texas mesonet site near New Home measured severe wind gusts from 1908 CST through 1913 CST. A peak wind gust of 70 mph was measured at 1911 CST.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: High pressure in the Gulf of Mexico produced breezy southerly winds over South Central Texas which led to a prescribed burn getting out of control in Bastrop County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A prescribed burn was scheduled for the Bastrop State Park at 11:30AM on the 18th. The planned burn included approximately 100 acres. At approximately 2:00PM Texas Department of Emergency Management Field Staff received a report that the burn was no longer controlled. No homes had been damaged and nearby homes in the area were evacuated. At the time the fire started relative humidity in the area was around 55% and winds were from the south at 16 mph with gusts to 25 mph. The fire was contained on the 24th having burned 812 acres.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level storm system brought a Pacific front through the combined Oklahoma and Texas Panhandles. The Pacific front brought westerly winds and dry air to the area. The pressure gradient along with strong winds aloft created breezy to windy sustained winds around 25 to 45 mph. With such strong winds aloft from this system many areas across the combined Panhandles experienced wind gusts between 58 and 64 mph. The strong winds combined with the extremely dry air, along with drought conditions in place, led to many wild fires breaking out across the area.  These fires impacted Hemphill, Hutchinson, and Roberts County. A total of 48,568 acres were burned and multiple structures along with farm equipment were lost to the fires.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Two different mesonet stations located across the county measured wind gusts between 60 and 61 mph between 1005 CST and 1038 CST.

Parts of South Central Texas received above normal rainfall in November including the northern Hill Country, the northern part of the I-35 corridor, and the Coastal Plains. Most of the rest of the area continued to have below normal rain. This had mixed results on the drought. Guadalupe County went from Exceptional (D4) drought to Extreme (D3) drought. Gonzales County went from D3 to Severe (D2) drought. Blanco and Kendall Counties went from D3 to D4 and Bandera, Gillespie, and Kerr went from D2 to D3. Comal and Hays stayed in D4, Bexar and Medina in D3, and Kinney in D2. Of the counties in D2 or worse drought Bandera, Bexar, and Comal had outdoor burn bans in effect at the end of the month. The 7-day average streamflow at the end of the month was below normal (10%-24%) on the Medina River and much below (<10%) normal on the Guadalupe River. The Edwards Aquifer rose 4.4 feet during the month, but was still 30.3 feet below average. Area reservoirs were below normal conservation pool elevation. Lake Amistad rose 0.8 feet, but will still 36.2 feet below normal. Lake Travis also rose 0.3 feet, but was 40.3 feet below normal. Medina Lake dropped 0.8 feet and was 78.8 feet below normal. Most public water systems encouraged at least voluntary water restrictions and many had mandatory restrictions in effect. Some the larger services had the following: New Braunfels Stage 1, San Antonio Stage 2, Austin Stage 1, and Kerrville Stage 1.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level storm system brought a Pacific front through the combined Oklahoma and Texas Panhandles. The Pacific front brought westerly winds and dry air to the area. The pressure gradient along with strong winds aloft created breezy to windy sustained winds around 25 to 45 mph. With such strong winds aloft from this system many areas across the combined Panhandles experienced wind gusts between 58 and 64 mph. The strong winds combined with the extremely dry air, along with drought conditions in place, led to many wild fires breaking out across the area.  These fires impacted Hemphill, Hutchinson, and Roberts County. A total of 48,568 acres were burned and multiple structures along with farm equipment were lost to the fires.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Both the AWOS located in Dumas and a mesonet station located 3 mile southeast of Dumas measured a wind gust of 59 mph a little over an hour apart.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Rainfall was a bit of a mixed bag in October. A swath of the central part of the area had 10-50% of normal. The area along the Rio Grande had 100-200% of normal. The rest of the area was in between. There was enough rainfall in Bandera County for that county to improve from Extreme (D3) drought to Severe (D2) drought. Lack of rain worsened the drought from D2 to D3 in Fayette and Gonzales Counties. All other counties remained where they were in September. Comal, Guadalupe, and Hays stayed in Exceptional (D4) drought. Bexar, Blanco, Caldwell, Kendall, and Medina remained in D3. Bastrop, Burnet, Gillespie, Kerr, Kinney, Lavaca, Llano, Real, Travis, Uvalde, Williamson, and Wilson stayed in D2. Of the counties in D2 or worse drought Comal, Guadalupe, Hays, Bexar, Blanco, Caldwell, Fayette, Gonzales, Kendall, Medina, Burnet, Gillespie, Llano, Travis, and Wilson had outdoor burn bans in effect at the end of the month. The 7-day average streamflow at the end of the month was normal (25%-75%) to below normal (10%-24%) on the Nueces River, much below normal (<10%) on the Frio River, below normal (10%-24%) on the Medina River, below normal (10%-24%) on the San Antonio River, much below normal (<10%) on the upper and lower Guadalupe River, and normal (25%-75%) to below normal (10%-24%) on the upper Colorado River. Area reservoirs were below normal pool level. Lake Amistad rose 4.5 feet, but was still 37.0 feel below normal. Medina Lake decreased 1.2 feet to 78.0 feet below normal and Lake Travis dropped 2.4 feet to 40.6 feet below normal. The Edwards Aquifer rose 2.3 feet, but was 33.2 feet below average. Most public water systems encouraged at least voluntary water restrictions and many had mandatory restrictions in effect. Some of the larger services had the following: New Braunfels Stage 1, San Antonio Stage 2, Austin Stage 1, and Kerrville Stage 1.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong upper level system moved through the combined Oklahoma and Texas Panhandles starting on the 21st and ending on the 22nd. This system brought precipitation in the form of rain and snow, and high winds. Winds were anywhere from 20 to 45 mph sustained, with gusts up to 64 mph. The night of the 21st, temperatures dropped to around 30 to 34 degrees Fahrenheit. Many areas stayed just above freezing with snow being very wet and heavy, which made it hard to be blown around by the wind but the snow stuck in tree branches and power lines leading to some damage and power outages mainly along portions of I-40 and along Highway 60 from Amarillo northeastward. There was a small corridor just south of the Canadian River Valley where 6 to 9 inches of snow fell by the morning of the 22nd.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A mesonet station located 3 miles NNE of Umbarger measured a wind gust of 58 mph at 1445 CST. This mesonet also had sustained winds of 40 to 45 mph between 1429 CST and 1607 CST.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Long term drought conditions continued to keep rangelands grassless putting a strain on ranchers, which have been forced to supplement feed or sell off cattle. Soil moisture continued to be short to very short for portions of the combined Panhandles through October. These soil conditions slowed the planting of winter wheat for some areas in the more extreme to exceptional drought conditions.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The far western quarter to third of the county started the month of October in Extreme Drought (D3) conditions. The rest of the county started the month off with Severe Drought (D2) conditions. With in the first week D3 conditions spread across much of the county with the far western portion developing Exceptional Drought (D4) conditions and stayed with these drought conditions through the end of the month with no improvements.  The county ended the month of October 0.5 to 1.5 below normal for the month. Also, the county remained in a 4 to 8 deficit year to date.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: Sherman County started the month with Severe Drought (D2) conditions in the southwestern two thirds. The northeastern third was in Extreme Drought (D3). Within the first couple of days of month the area of D3 in the northeast degraded into Exceptional Drought (D4) conditions and all but the southwest corner of D2 degraded into D3 conditions. With the exception of the southwest corner that ended the month with near normal rainfall, the rest of the county ended the month of October 0.5 to 1.5 below normal for the month. The majority of the county remained in a 6 to 10 deficit year to date.

With much of the county receiving below normal rainfall for the month these drought conditions stayed through the entire month. The county remained in a 6 to 10 deficit year to date.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Dry conditions continued since August of 2021 with only a few isolated events bringing minimal precipitation to the combined Oklahoma and Texas Panhandles. Soil moisture remained short to very short with supplemental feeding required for cattle with bare pastures. Other concerns for ranchers was the threat of wildfires. Tillage and winter wheat needed irrigation in order to thrive. These drought conditions contributed to multiple wildfires when combined with high wind days and low relative humidity. Across the combined Texas and Oklahoma Panhandles, a total of 51082 acres were burned with 35 structures and 11 vehicles lost due to the fires.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Ochiltree County started the month in extreme (D3) drought. By mid month the entire county fell into exceptional (D4) drought. A late month storm system helped the county improve back to extreme drought by the 22nd. Northern portions of the county remained in a 4 to 10 deficit over the past 365 days. The rest of the county remained in a 4 to 6 deficit over the past 365 days.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: Hutchinson County started the month in extreme (D3) drought conditions. By the end of the first week the entire county fell into exceptional (D4) drought conditions. A late month snow storm brough some needed relief and brought at least one categorical improvement to all but the far northwest corner of the county. The far southeast corner of the county improved two categorical improvements back to severe (D2) drought. The county remained in a 2 to 6 deficit going back 365 days. The drought conditions also contributed to a wildfire that burned 1500 acres on the 29th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level storm system brought a Pacific front through the combined Oklahoma and Texas Panhandles. The Pacific front brought westerly winds and dry air to the area. The pressure gradient along with strong winds aloft created breezy to windy sustained winds around 25 to 45 mph. With such strong winds aloft from this system many areas across the combined Panhandles experienced wind gusts between 58 and 64 mph. The strong winds combined with the extremely dry air, along with drought conditions in place, led to many wild fires breaking out across the area.  These fires impacted Hemphill, Hutchinson, and Roberts County. A total of 48,568 acres were burned and multiple structures along with farm equipment were lost to the fires.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The ASOS located at the Amarillo Airport measured a wind gust of 58 mph at 1324 CST.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong upper level system moved through the combined Oklahoma and Texas Panhandles starting on the 21st and ending on the 22nd. This system brought precipitation in the form of rain and snow, and high winds. Winds were anywhere from 20 to 45 mph sustained, with gusts up to 64 mph. The night of the 21st, temperatures dropped to around 30 to 34 degrees Fahrenheit. Many areas stayed just above freezing with snow being very wet and heavy, which made it hard to be blown around by the wind but the snow stuck in tree branches and power lines leading to some damage and power outages mainly along portions of I-40 and along Highway 60 from Amarillo northeastward. There was a small corridor just south of the Canadian River Valley where 6 to 9 inches of snow fell by the morning of the 22nd.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A mesonet station locasted near Dumas measured sustained winds between 40 and 47 mph between 1450 CST and 1819 CST.

Soil moisture continued to be short to very short for portions of the combined Panhandles through October. A long lasting deficit contributed to the north to northeastern half or so of the county developed Extreme Drought (D3) and the expansion of D2 across the rest of the southern half of the county.  Much of the county remained in a 4 to 8 deficit year to date at the end of October.

Dry conditions continued since August of 2021 with only a few isolated events bringing minimal precipitation to the combined Oklahoma and Texas Panhandles. Soil moisture remained short to very short with supplemental feeding required for cattle with bare pastures. Other concerns for ranchers was the threat of wildfires. Tillage and winter wheat needed irrigation in order to thrive. These drought conditions contributed to multiple wildfires when combined with high wind days and low relative humidity. Across the combined Texas and Oklahoma Panhandles, a total of 51082 acres were burned with 35 structures and 11 vehicles lost due to the fires.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Oldham County started the month in extreme (D3) drought conditions. During the third week a storm system moved through improving the south to southeast two thirds of county and ending the month in severe (D2) drought. The county ended the month in 4 to 6 deficit dating back 365 days.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A broad fetch of Pacific moisture streamed over much of Texas ahead of a broad mid-upper level trough gradually approaching via the Rockies. However, winter wheat has been very poor to this date. Furthermore, livestock was being fed supplemental feed due to poor native grasslands.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A slow moving cold front moved through extreme Southeast Oklahoma shortly after daybreak on February 2nd, and into Northeast Texas and Southwest Arkansas through the afternoon. However, the deeper colder air was dammed up in the Ouachita Mountains of Southeast Oklahoma and Western Arkansas, with temperatures slowly falling to and below freezing across much of East Texas during the day on the 3rd. Meanwhile, a longwave trough moved into West Texas and Western Oklahoma during the daytime hours on the 2nd, with areas of sleet and snow developing ahead of the trough over much of Oklahoma and Texas. While the precipitation started off as rain across East Texas early on the 3rd, it eventually transitioned over to a mixture of freezing rain, sleet, and snow, with ice accumulations ranging from a glazing to just over one-tenth of an inch, and a dusting of snow reported. Icing of bridges and overpasses were common across East Texas mainly during the afternoon and evening. ||In Cherokee County, 0.13 inches of ice was recorded 6 E of New Summerfield.|In Gregg County, 3 NW of Longview recorded 0.1 inches of snow, as did 2 W of Longview.

The coldest period was between the night of February 4th through the morning of February 5th when clouds cleared out and temperatures dropped into the lower to middle 20s across portions of Deep South Texas, with the coldest readings in rural inland locations away from the populated Rio Grande Valley. Much of the region away from the populated Rio Grande Valley experienced another light freeze the morning of February 6th. Wind chills dipped into the middle teens to middle 20s the morning of February 4th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Temperatures fell below freezing around 1:15AM CST on February 5th, and did not rise above freezing until 8:55AM CST. The Brooks County Airport (KBKS) observed a low of 25 degrees.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong pressure gradient between a surface low over the Panhandle of Texas and a strong high off the Carolina Coastline allowed very strong southerly flow to develop the morning of February 16th and continue through the early evening. Highest peak wind speeds of 30 to 52 mph were reported across Deep South Texas and the Rio Grande Valley, with the highest reports along the eastern half of this area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tight pressure gradient between a surface high pressure off the Carolina Coast and a low pressure system over the Panhandle of Texas resulted in very windy conditions across the Rio Grande Valley throughout the day on February 16th. An estimated gust of 45 knots early in the afternoon damaged the metal roof of the Boys and Girls Club in San Benito. This caused an estimated $10,000 worth of damage and kept them to closed for the remainder of the week. Sporadic power outages were also reported across portions of Cameron County. |Note: 45 knots is equivalent to 52 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A southwest to northeast oriented trough was moving through the region with a strong surface low over eastern New Mexico. West to southwest winds gusted up to 59 mph as the system moved through which produced some downed power lines.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The El Paso Airport reported a peak gust of 59 mph.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A slow moving cold front moved through extreme Southeast Oklahoma shortly after daybreak on February 2nd, and into Northeast Texas and Southwest Arkansas through the afternoon. However, the deeper colder air was dammed up in the Ouachita Mountains of Southeast Oklahoma and Western Arkansas, with temperatures slowly falling to and below freezing across much of East Texas during the day on the 3rd. Meanwhile, a longwave trough moved into West Texas and Western Oklahoma during the daytime hours on the 2nd, with areas of sleet and snow developing ahead of the trough over much of Oklahoma and Texas. While the precipitation started off as rain across East Texas early on the 3rd, it eventually transitioned over to a mixture of freezing rain, sleet, and snow, with ice accumulations ranging from a glazing to just over one-tenth of an inch, and a dusting of snow reported. Icing of bridges and overpasses were common across East Texas mainly during the afternoon and evening. ||In Cherokee County, 0.13 inches of ice was recorded 6 E of New Summerfield.|In Gregg County, 3 NW of Longview recorded 0.1 inches of snow, as did 2 W of Longview.

Extreme drought (D3) conditions remained nearly unchanged during the month of February. Parmer County in the extreme southwestern Texas Panhandle was added to D3 drought conditions. Moderate (D1) to Severe (D2) drought conditions were observed elsewhere across the remainder of the region.||These drought conditions were strongly tied to a mature moderate strength La Ni��a over the tropical eastern Pacific Ocean. Several drier than average months have led to these conditions. The latest three month precipitation amounts continued to range from 5% to 25% of normal. A minor winter weather event occurred around February 4-5 which brought mostly light snowfall to the region. Heavy snowfall was observed in the southern Rolling Plains with light snowfall elsewhere. February also saw a few days of extremely cold temperatures around this same time frame with some locations observing their coldest temperatures in nearly 30 years. However, the months of December, January, and February are the peak of the dry season. There are few agricultural impacts this time of year with most of the area cotton already harvested. However, winter wheat has been very poor to this date. Furthermore, livestock was being fed supplemental feed due to poor native grasslands.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Conditions were favorable for wildfire spread in the wake of a strong cold front the afternoon of February 12th. Strong, gusty winds combined with cured ground fuels from various freeze events from the previous weeks allowed for rapid wildfire growth. The Polo Fire, in the center of Kenedy County, ignited on February 12th around 4:00PM CST and continued until the middle of the afternoon on February 13th when it was 100% contained. The fire consumed a total of 3,628.8 acres.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The event known as the Polo Fire was estimated to have initiated around 3:00PM CST just south of Armstrong, TX east of Highway 77 and burned until the middle of the afternoon on the 13th, when it was announced to be 100% contained by 5:19PM CST. This wildfire consumed a total of 3,628.8 acres. A spot request submitted by the Texas A&M Fire Service and an NWS Employee���s report at 4:45PM CST about smelling smoke in the Harlingen area on February 12th were used as a guide for the earlier ignition and the very rapid spread that followed.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Conditions were very favorable for wildfire spread ahead of a cold front during the day of February 16th. Strong, gusty southerly winds combined with cured ground fuels from several freeze events from the previous weeks allowed for rapid wildfire growth. The 755 wildfire, in the south central portion of the county, ignited on February 16th around 2:00PM CST and continued until 1:00PM CST on February 18th when it was announced it was 100 percent contained. The fire consumed a total of 2,000 acres.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The event known as the 755 Wildfire was estimated to have initiated around 2:00PM CST south of Encino, TX near the intersection of US-281 and FM 755. It burned until the afternoon of the 18th when it was announced to be 100 percent contained at 2:00PM CST. This wildfire consumed a total of 2,000 acres. A Spot Request submitted by the Texas A&M Fire Service on February 16th and the GOES-16 Day Land Cloud Fire RGB channel were used as a guide for the ignition time and very rapid spread that followed.

As this wave moved over the area, it provided enough lift to develop wintry precipitation over the southern Texas Panhandle. Early on in the event on the 12th, the lower atmosphere was relatively dry, therefore the onset of precipitation was delayed until saturation occurred. Extreme drought (D3) conditions remained nearly unchanged during the month of February. Parmer County in the extreme southwestern Texas Panhandle was added to D3 drought conditions. Moderate (D1) to Severe (D2) drought conditions were observed elsewhere across the remainder of the region.||These drought conditions were strongly tied to a mature moderate strength La Ni��a over the tropical eastern Pacific Ocean. Several drier than average months have led to these conditions. The latest three month precipitation amounts continued to range from 5% to 25% of normal. A minor winter weather event occurred around February 4-5 which brought mostly light snowfall to the region. Heavy snowfall was observed in the southern Rolling Plains with light snowfall elsewhere. February also saw a few days of extremely cold temperatures around this same time frame with some locations observing their coldest temperatures in nearly 30 years. However, the months of December, January, and February are the peak of the dry season. There are few agricultural impacts this time of year with most of the area cotton already harvested. However, winter wheat has been very poor to this date. Furthermore, livestock was being fed supplemental feed due to poor native grasslands.

Dry conditions continued since August of 2021 with only a few isolated events bringing minimal precipitation to the combined Oklahoma and Texas Panhandles. Soil moisture remained short to very short with supplemental feeding required for cattle with bare pastures. Other concerns for ranchers was the threat of wildfires. Tillage and winter wheat needed irrigation in order to thrive. These drought conditions contributed to multiple wildfires when combined with high wind days and low relative humidity. Across the combined Texas and Oklahoma Panhandles, a total of 51082 acres were burned with 35 structures and 11 vehicles lost due to the fires.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Deaf Smith County started the month in extreme (D3) drought conditions. Most of the county remained in extreme drought by the end of the month with many areas only receiving 0.25 to 0.5 of precipitation during the month. The northwestern and northeastern corner of the county received closer to 0.75 to 1 allowing for these isolated areas of the county to improve to severe (D2) drought status by the end of the month.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several agencies conducted rescue operations for cold stunned green sea turtles along the Middle Texas coast. In the Espiritu Santo Bay and San Antonio Bay area, 15 green sea turtles were rescued.

A 47-yo gentleman was found deceased in a home that had lost power, and the resident was using propane to provide heat.

Meanwhile, a longwave trough moved into West Texas and Western Oklahoma during the daytime hours on the 2nd, with areas of sleet and snow developing ahead of the trough over much of Oklahoma and Texas. While the precipitation started off as rain across Northeast Texas early on the 3rd, it eventually transitioned over to a mixture of freezing rain, sleet, and snow, with ice accumulations ranging from a glazing to just under one-quarter inch, and a dusting of snow reported. This resulted in hazardous travel conditions over bridges and overpasses and some secondary roadways across Northeast Texas. ||In Franklin County, 1 N of Mount Vernon reported 0.10 inches of ice. |In Upshur County, 7 SSW Ore City and Diana recorded 0.10 inches of ice, with 6 ENE Gilmer and Union Grove both recording a glaze of ice. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Soils remained dry to very dry. Although some precipitation fell during the month of January, it was not enough to keep drought conditions from worsening. Some winter wheat was irrigated on warm days although farmers struggle to decide what to do to maximize output while limiting input. High fertilizer prices did not make this easy as the drought conditions continued to deteriorate naturally occurring nitrogen in the soil. Ranchers had to continue supplemental feeding as rangelands remained dormant. On top of the agricultural impacts from extreme to exceptional drought conditions, conditions favorable for wildfires remained a threat to the combined Oklahoma and Texas Panhandles.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Collingsworth County went into the month of January with the northeast half of the county in extreme drought (D3). Within the first few days of the month the rest of the county that was in severe drought (D2) slipped into extreme drought as well and stayed through the end of the month. The county ended the month in a 4 to 8 inch deficit over the past 180 days.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong upper level low pressure system moved over the parts of the Central Plains and over the combined Oklahoma/Texas Panhandles as well as the rest of the Oklahoma Panhandle. This system brought a strong cold front at the surface early in the day on Friday the 14th of January.  Sustained winds reached 40 plus mph across multiple counties in the area.  With drought conditions persisting across the area, these high winds fueled a couple of wildfires as well as created reduced visibilities due to blowing dust. One of fires in the area threatened the town of Stinnett, TX. Wind gust upwards of 58 to 68 mph were recorded across the combined Panhandles during the afternoon into evening on the 14th. Over night winds continued strong with some areas gusting over 60 mph until the early morning hours on the 15th in some areas. Extreme drought conditions along with strong southwesterly winds and low relative humidity values contributed to a large wildfire which occurred in the central Texas Panhandle.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Arctic air mass surged into south Texas on February 3rd and continued through the 5th. Areas of freezing rain and sleet occurred over the Victoria Crossroads on the afternoon and evening of the 3rd. Temperatures fell by the morning of the 4th to the lower 20s in the Victoria Crossroads to around 30 along the coast and along the Rio Grande. With strong winds, wind chill temperatures fell to around 10 degrees to the upper teens on the morning of the 4th. Arctic air remained over the region on the 4th with temperatures falling to the upper teens to upper 20s on the morning of the 5th. The long duration cold spell affected the green turtle population along the Middle Texas coast. Agencies rescued cold stunned turtles along the coast. Over 220 green turtles were rescued while 8 turtles were found dead. A boil water notice was issued for the North Victoria Utilities due to power outage that affected 234 people. The City of Corpus Christi performed over 800 welfare checks. Sixty five people were transported to Robstown to shelter at the Richard M. Borchard Fairgrounds. The Harbor Bridge was closed due to ice accumulations on the bridge on the 4th.  A pipe burst at a hospital caused damage to equipment in Alice.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Temperatures fell into the mid to upper 20s on the 4th and 5th over coastal Refugio County. Wind chill temperatures ranged from 10 to 15 degrees during the morning hours of the 4th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe (D2) drought conditions persisted across much of East and Northeast Texas throughout February. This was in response to a prolonged period of dryness which began back in mid-summer 2021, coupled with above normal temperatures which persisted through much of the fall and early winter. Total rainfall amounts generally between 10-12 inches fell across these areas from August through December, which was around 50% or less of normal. Total rainfall in January was generally below average across these areas but increased in February to between 2-4 inches. This dryness contributed to lower than normal streamflow observed across area creeks, streams, and rivers.

Scattered thunderstorms associated with the approach of an offshore low pressure system produced several tornadoes on the evening of January 8 and the early morning of January 9. These tornadoes resulted in several instances of property and tree damage across the Greater Houston Area. Some non-tornadic storms also produced strong, damaging wind gusts. Later, heavy rainfall associated with continuing thunderstorm activity resulted in flash flooding across the Houston Metro.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Widespread flooding was reported along Brickhouse Gully in the Oak Forest neighborhood. Roadways were made impassable by floodwaters.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe (D2) drought conditions expanded across portions of east and northeast Texas through the month of January. This was in response to a prolonged period of dryness which began back in mid summer 2021, coupled with above normal temperatures which persisted through much of the Fall and all of December. Total rainfall amounts generally between 10-12 inches fell across these areas from August through December, which was around 50% or less of normal. Total rainfall in January generally averaged between an inch to two inches across much of east and northeast Texas. This dryness contributed to lower than normal streamflow observed across area creeks, streams, and rivers across the area.

Soils remained dry to very dry. Although some precipitation fell during the month of January, it was not enough to keep drought conditions from worsening. Some winter wheat was irrigated on warm days although farmers struggle to decide what to do to maximize output while limiting input. High fertilizer prices did not make this easy as the drought conditions continued to deteriorate naturally occurring nitrogen in the soil. Ranchers had to continue supplemental feeding as rangelands remained dormant. On top of the agricultural impacts from extreme to exceptional drought conditions, conditions favorable for wildfires remained a threat to the combined Oklahoma and Texas Panhandles.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Lipscomb County ended December with close to 60 days straight with no precipitation and the entire county in severe drought (D2). Though some precipitation fell on the first of January, it was not enough to prevent the county from slipping into extreme drought (D3) the during the first few days of January. The county remained in D3 through the entire month as the monthly total precipitation was only around a tenth of an inch, and the county remained in a 2 to 6 inch deficit over the previous 180 days.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong upper level low pressure system moved over the parts of the Central Plains and over the combined Oklahoma/Texas Panhandles as well as the rest of the Oklahoma Panhandle. This system brought a strong cold front at the surface early in the day on Friday the 14th of January.  Sustained winds reached 40 plus mph across multiple counties in the area.  With drought conditions persisting across the area, these high winds fueled a couple of wildfires as well as created reduced visibilities due to blowing dust. One of fires in the area threatened the town of Stinnett, TX. Wind gust upwards of 58 to 68 mph were recorded across the combined Panhandles during the afternoon into evening on the 14th. Over night winds continued strong with some areas gusting over 60 mph until the early morning hours on the 15th in some areas. Extreme drought conditions along with strong southwesterly winds and low relative humidity values contributed to a large wildfire which occurred in the central Texas Panhandle.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A period of freezing rain created a thin layer of ice or glaze over portions of the lower Rio Grande Valley between 5AM CST and 9:30AM CST the morning of January 21st. This rare occurrence led to several reports of trees and vegetation glazed with a layer of ice. Most glaze reports were centered around the Los Fresnos, Rio Hondo, and Harlingen areas in Cameron County with other reports just south of Raymondville in Willacy County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Freezing rain likely fell for a brief period between 3:55AM CST and 5:55AM CST near Falfurrias in Brooks County. This is inferred due to the Brooks County Airport (KBKS) reporting a temperature of 30.7 degrees with accumulating precipitation with radar returns overhead.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The morning of January 20th saw a cold front sweep through the Rio Grande Valley and Deep South Texas. As 1045 mb high moved out of Canada and pushed temperatures lower throughout the day on the 20th. An upper-level low moving overhead provided enough lift to allow widespread showers to form the night of the 20th into the morning of January 21st. All of this contributed to temperatures touching the freezing mark in numerous locations from Jim Hogg southeast through Cameron County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Temperatures fell to freezing around 2:15 AM on January 21st and remained at or below freezing until 8:55 AM. Low temperatures fell into the lower 30s across the area. A minimum temperature of 31 degrees was observed at the Brooks County Airport (KBKS).

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Arctic air mass surged into south Texas on February 3rd and continued through the 5th. Areas of freezing rain and sleet occurred over the Victoria Crossroads on the afternoon and evening of the 3rd. Temperatures fell by the morning of the 4th to the lower 20s in the Victoria Crossroads to around 30 along the coast and along the Rio Grande. With strong winds, wind chill temperatures fell to around 10 degrees to the upper teens on the morning of the 4th. Arctic air remained over the region on the 4th with temperatures falling to the upper teens to upper 20s on the morning of the 5th. The long duration cold spell affected the green turtle population along the Middle Texas coast. Agencies rescued cold stunned turtles along the coast. Over 220 green turtles were rescued while 8 turtles were found dead. A boil water notice was issued for the North Victoria Utilities due to power outage that affected 234 people. The City of Corpus Christi performed over 800 welfare checks. Sixty five people were transported to Robstown to shelter at the Richard M. Borchard Fairgrounds. The Harbor Bridge was closed due to ice accumulations on the bridge on the 4th.  A pipe burst at a hospital caused damage to equipment in Alice.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Temperatures fell into the upper 20s on the 4th and 5th over inland San Patricio County. Wind chill temperatures ranged from 10 to 15 degrees during the morning hours of the 4th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The morning of January 20th saw a cold front sweep through the Rio Grande Valley and Deep South Texas. As 1045 mb high moved out of Canada and pushed temperatures lower throughout the day on the 20th. An upper-level low moving overhead provided enough lift to allow widespread showers to form the night of the 20th into the morning of January 21st. All of this contributed to temperatures touching the freezing mark in numerous locations from Jim Hogg southeast through Cameron County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Temperatures fell to freezing around 1:16AM CST on January 21st and remained near freezing until 8:47AM CST. Low temperatures fell into the lower 30s across the area. A minimum temperature of 31 degrees was observed at the Union Pacific Railroad Station 8 miles south of Armstrong (UR074).

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Arctic air mass surged into south Texas on February 3rd and continued through the 5th. Areas of freezing rain and sleet occurred over the Victoria Crossroads on the afternoon and evening of the 3rd. Temperatures fell by the morning of the 4th to the lower 20s in the Victoria Crossroads to around 30 along the coast and along the Rio Grande. With strong winds, wind chill temperatures fell to around 10 degrees to the upper teens on the morning of the 4th. Arctic air remained over the region on the 4th with temperatures falling to the upper teens to upper 20s on the morning of the 5th. The long duration cold spell affected the green turtle population along the Middle Texas coast. Agencies rescued cold stunned turtles along the coast. Over 220 green turtles were rescued while 8 turtles were found dead. A boil water notice was issued for the North Victoria Utilities due to power outage that affected 234 people. The City of Corpus Christi performed over 800 welfare checks. Sixty five people were transported to Robstown to shelter at the Richard M. Borchard Fairgrounds. The Harbor Bridge was closed due to ice accumulations on the bridge on the 4th.  A pipe burst at a hospital caused damage to equipment in Alice.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Temperatures fell into the upper 20s on the 4th and 5th over islands of Nueces County. Wind chill temperatures ranged from 12 to 15 degrees during the morning hours of the 4th.

A strong upper level low pressure system moved over the parts of the Central Plains and over the combined Oklahoma/Texas Panhandles as well as the rest of the Oklahoma Panhandle. This system brought a strong cold front at the surface early in the day on Friday the 14th of January.  Sustained winds reached 40 plus mph across multiple counties in the area.  With drought conditions persisting across the area, these high winds fueled a couple of wildfires as well as created reduced visibilities due to blowing dust. One of fires in the area threatened the town of Stinnett, TX. Wind gust upwards of 58 to 68 mph were recorded across the combined Panhandles during the afternoon into evening on the 14th. Over night winds continued strong with some areas gusting over 60 mph until the early morning hours on the 15th in some areas. Extreme drought conditions along with strong southwesterly winds and low relative humidity values contributed to a large wildfire which occurred in the central Texas Panhandle.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Carbon Camp fire began 1 mile southeast of Stinnett, Texas in Hutchinson County. The Carbon Camp fire began just south of Carbon Camp Road and spread south towards the Scotts Acres subdivision. Evacuations were in place for the residents of Scotts Acres subdivision in Stinnett, Texas. State Highway 136 was shut down for a period of time. There was a report of as many as 85 structures threatened. Three structures or properties, one occupied home, one barn and an RV, were lost. However, there were no reports of any injuries or fatalities. The fire consumed 177 acres and was contained as of 1300CST on January 15, 2022. Multiple local fire departments from Stinnett VFD, Crutch VFD, Fritch VFD, Borger FD, Potter County FD, Skellytown VFD, responded to assist along with National Parks Service (NPS), Pantex and State resources from the Texas A&M Forest Service (TAMFS). TAMFS and Stinnett Fire Department worked in unified command. Aircraft was ordered but canceled.

A strong winter storm system brought some really dry snow and below freezing temperatures to the combined Oklahoma and Texas Panhandles during the first week of February. Much of the area stayed below freezing February 2nd through the early morning on February 4th and temperatures barely rose above freezing the afternoon of the 4th. Wind chill values dropped to the -5 to -20 range for several hours between February 2nd through early morning on the 3rd as winds blew 15 to 25 mph with gusts up to 30 mph at times with this storm system. Temperatures were very cold on the night of the 3rd into the morning of the 4th as winds became light. Most of the snow fell over a 48 hour period starting on the 2nd through the 3rd. Although some isolated areas received upwards of 6 inches of snow during a 24 hour period. Most of the area received 4 to 6 inches of snow over a 48 hour period. This storm system did take two lives, one direct and one indirect due to the extremely cold wind chills.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A Co-op observer, located near Perryton, TX, recorded a trace of snow in the 24 hours preceding 0600 CST on the 2nd. Then 4 of snow in the 24 hrs preceding 0600 CST on the 3rd. An additional 2 of snow was measured in the 24 hrs preceeding 0600 CST on the 4th.

A strong winter storm system brought some really dry snow and below freezing temperatures to the combined Oklahoma and Texas Panhandles during the first week of February. Much of the area stayed below freezing February 2nd through the early morning on February 4th and temperatures barely rose above freezing the afternoon of the 4th. Wind chill values dropped to the -5 to -20 range for several hours between February 2nd through early morning on the 3rd as winds blew 15 to 25 mph with gusts up to 30 mph at times with this storm system. Temperatures were very cold on the night of the 3rd into the morning of the 4th as winds became light. Most of the snow fell over a 48 hour period starting on the 2nd through the 3rd. Although some isolated areas received upwards of 6 inches of snow during a 24 hour period. Most of the area received 4 to 6 inches of snow over a 48 hour period. This storm system did take two lives, one direct and one indirect due to the extremely cold wind chills.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wind chill values fell into the minus 15 to minus 20 degree range on the morning of the 3rd. Although the mesonet near Borger measured close to or right around minus 15 for several hours, the mesonet located near Stinnett measured wind chill values well into the minus 15 to minus 20 range for about 12 hours straight.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong upper level low pressure system tracked east across the Red River Valley of Southern Oklahoma and North Texas during the afternoon of January 8th, before shifting across Northeast Texas into Southwest Arkansas during the early morning hours of the 9th. Ahead of this low, strong southerly low level winds rapidly transported low level moisture back north across the region, with large scale forcing and elevated instability ahead of the low contributing to areas of showers and embedded thunderstorms over East Texas, North Louisiana, and Southwest Arkansas. An isolated severe thunderstorm developed during the afternoon of the 8th over Nacogdoches County in East Texas, producing ping pong ball size hail just southeast of Nacogdoches. Meanwhile, a warm front spread north into portions of Deep East Texas and Central Louisiana during the late evening and early morning hours, with increasing instability and low level wind shear fueling the development of strong to severe thunderstorms over these areas. These storms produced damaging winds which downed trees and limbs in Sabine County, with additional severe storms later spawning two tornadoes in Southern Sabine Parish, Louisiana. These storms also continued to develop and move repeatedly over the same areas during the early morning hours across extreme Southeast Angelina, Southern San Augustine, and Central Sabine Counties, producing a narrow swath of heavy rain with amounts ranging from 3-7+ inches. This resulted in extensive flash flooding across Southern San Augustine and Central Sabine Counties, before the storms shifted east into West Central Louisiana just prior to daybreak on the 9th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Ping pong ball size hail fell off of East Main Street near Nottingham and Robin Hood Drives.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Soils remained dry to very dry. Although some precipitation fell during the month of January, it was not enough to keep drought conditions from worsening. Some winter wheat was irrigated on warm days although farmers struggle to decide what to do to maximize output while limiting input. High fertilizer prices did not make this easy as the drought conditions continued to deteriorate naturally occurring nitrogen in the soil. Ranchers had to continue supplemental feeding as rangelands remained dormant. On top of the agricultural impacts from extreme to exceptional drought conditions, conditions favorable for wildfires remained a threat to the combined Oklahoma and Texas Panhandles.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Dallam County entered the month of January with the majority of the extreme drought (D3), with the exception of the far southwest corner of the county was in severe drought (D2). By mid month the area of severe drought slipped into extreme drought.  Dallam County went 79 to 80 days straight without precipitation going into the month of January. This streak of no measurable precipitation ended on the first. However, the month only ended with a few hundredths of an inch of liquid which was not enough to improve already dire conditions. The county still remained in a  4 to 8 inch deficit over the previous 12 months.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Arctic air mass surged into south Texas on February 3rd and continued through the 5th. Areas of freezing rain and sleet occurred over the Victoria Crossroads on the afternoon and evening of the 3rd. Temperatures fell by the morning of the 4th to the lower 20s in the Victoria Crossroads to around 30 along the coast and along the Rio Grande. With strong winds, wind chill temperatures fell to around 10 degrees to the upper teens on the morning of the 4th. Arctic air remained over the region on the 4th with temperatures falling to the upper teens to upper 20s on the morning of the 5th. The long duration cold spell affected the green turtle population along the Middle Texas coast. Agencies rescued cold stunned turtles along the coast. Over 220 green turtles were rescued while 8 turtles were found dead. A boil water notice was issued for the North Victoria Utilities due to power outage that affected 234 people. The City of Corpus Christi performed over 800 welfare checks. Sixty five people were transported to Robstown to shelter at the Richard M. Borchard Fairgrounds. The Harbor Bridge was closed due to ice accumulations on the bridge on the 4th.  A pipe burst at a hospital caused damage to equipment in Alice.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Temperatures fell into the upper 20s on the 4th and the lower 20s on the 5th over La Salle County. Wind chill temperatures were in the upper teens during the morning hours of the 4th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong winter storm system brought some really dry snow and below freezing temperatures to the combined Oklahoma and Texas Panhandles during the first week of February. Wind chill values dropped to the -5 to -20 range for several hours between February 2nd through early morning on the 3rd as winds blew 15 to 25 mph with gusts up to 30 mph at times with this storm system. This storm system did take two lives, one direct and one indirect due to the extremely cold wind chills.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong upper level low pressure system tracked east across the Red River Valley of Southern Oklahoma and North Texas during the afternoon of January 8th, before shifting across Northeast Texas into Southwest Arkansas during the early morning hours of the 9th. Ahead of this low, strong southerly low level winds rapidly transported low level moisture back north across the region, with large scale forcing and elevated instability ahead of the low contributing to areas of showers and embedded thunderstorms over East Texas, North Louisiana, and Southwest Arkansas. An isolated severe thunderstorm developed during the afternoon of the 8th over Nacogdoches County in East Texas, producing ping pong ball size hail just southeast of Nacogdoches. Meanwhile, a warm front spread north into portions of Deep East Texas and Central Louisiana during the late evening and early morning hours, with increasing instability and low level wind shear fueling the development of strong to severe thunderstorms over these areas. These storms produced damaging winds which downed trees and limbs in Sabine County, with additional severe storms later spawning two tornadoes in Southern Sabine Parish, Louisiana. These storms also continued to develop and move repeatedly over the same areas during the early morning hours across extreme Southeast Angelina, Southern San Augustine, and Central Sabine Counties, producing a narrow swath of heavy rain with amounts ranging from 3-7+ inches. This resulted in extensive flash flooding across Southern San Augustine and Central Sabine Counties, before the storms shifted east into West Central Louisiana just prior to daybreak on the 9th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Large limbs were blown down near the intersection of Highway 3382 and Old Sabinetown Road in the Lowe's Creek community.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe (D2) drought conditions continued across portions of east and northeast Texas through the month of January.  This was in response to a prolonged period of dryness which began back in mid summer 2021, coupled with above normal temperatures which persisted through much of the Fall and all of December. Total rainfall amounts generally between 10-12 inches fell across these areas from August through December, which was around 50% or less of normal. Total rainfall in January generally averaged between an inch to two inches across much of east and northeast Texas. This dryness contributed to lower than normal streamflow observed across area creeks, streams, and rivers across the area.

Soils remained dry to very dry. Although some precipitation fell during the month of January, it was not enough to keep drought conditions from worsening. Some winter wheat was irrigated on warm days although farmers struggle to decide what to do to maximize output while limiting input. High fertilizer prices did not make this easy as the drought conditions continued to deteriorate naturally occurring nitrogen in the soil. Ranchers had to continue supplemental feeding as rangelands remained dormant. On top of the agricultural impacts from extreme to exceptional drought conditions, conditions favorable for wildfires remained a threat to the combined Oklahoma and Texas Panhandles.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong upper level low pressure system moved over the parts of the Central Plains and over the combined Oklahoma/Texas Panhandles as well as the rest of the Oklahoma Panhandle. This system brought a strong cold front at the surface early in the day on Friday the 14th of January.  Sustained winds reached 40 plus mph across multiple counties in the area.  With drought conditions persisting across the area, these high winds fueled a couple of wildfires as well as created reduced visibilities due to blowing dust. One of fires in the area threatened the town of Stinnett, TX. Wind gust upwards of 58 to 68 mph were recorded across the combined Panhandles during the afternoon into evening on the 14th. Over night winds continued strong with some areas gusting over 60 mph until the early morning hours on the 15th in some areas. Extreme drought conditions along with strong southwesterly winds and low relative humidity values contributed to a large wildfire which occurred in the central Texas Panhandle.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The mesonet located 7 miles east of Borger measured a wind gust of 58 mph first at 1431 CST. The ASOS located at the Borger aiport measured a winds gust of 63 mph at 1538 CST. Finally the mesonet station located 2 miles north of Stinnett measured a gust of 59 mph at 1641 CST.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A cool and very dry airmass settled in over the Rio Grande Valley and Deep South Texas following a cold front that arrived early on January 2nd. Arctic air was pushed south by a 1034mb high that settled over northern Texas. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A slow moving cold front moved through extreme Southeast Oklahoma shortly after daybreak on February 2nd, and into Northeast Texas and Southwest Arkansas through the afternoon. However, the deeper colder air was dammed up in the Ouachita Mountains of Southeast Oklahoma and Western Arkansas, with temperatures slowly falling to and below freezing across much of extreme Northeast Texas during the early morning hours on the 3rd. Meanwhile, a longwave trough moved into West Texas and Western Oklahoma during the daytime hours on the 2nd, with areas of sleet and snow developing ahead of the trough over much of Oklahoma and Texas. While the precipitation started off as rain across Northeast Texas, it eventually transitioned over to a mixture of freezing rain, sleet, and snow, with sleet accumulations of up to a half-inch across Western Wood County near Quitman, and a dusting at most of snow reported. ||An observer 1 mile west-northwest of Quitman measured 0.5 inches of sleet, with sleet accumulations of 0.1 inches measured at Mineola. This resulted in ice accumulations on bridges and roadways, which made travel extremely hazardous over Western Wood County. A CoCoRaHS observer 2.6 miles north of Hawkins recorded 0.5 inches of snow.

A strong winter storm system brought some really dry snow and below freezing temperatures to the combined Oklahoma and Texas Panhandles during the first week of February. Much of the area stayed below freezing February 2nd through the early morning on February 4th and temperatures barely rose above freezing the afternoon of the 4th. Wind chill values dropped to the -5 to -20 range for several hours between February 2nd through early morning on the 3rd as winds blew 15 to 25 mph with gusts up to 30 mph at times with this storm system. Temperatures were very cold on the night of the 3rd into the morning of the 4th as winds became light. Most of the snow fell over a 48 hour period starting on the 2nd through the 3rd. Although some isolated areas received upwards of 6 inches of snow during a 24 hour period. Most of the area received 4 to 6 inches of snow over a 48 hour period. This storm system did take two lives, one direct and one indirect due to the extremely cold wind chills.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A CoCoRaHS observer located 9 miles SW of of Amarillo reported several inches of snow between February 2nd through 4th.  Two inches of snow fell during the 24 hours preceding 0700 CST on the third.  Another 2.2 inches fell during the 24 hour period preceding 0700 CST on the fourth.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe (D2) drought conditions continued across portions of east and northeast Texas through the month of January.
