A phenomenon known as a heat burst occurred 9 miles north-northwest of Waka, TX. This occurs when anvil rains from dissipating showers/thunderstorms cause hot dry air loft to sink to the surface through somewhat of a dry downburst process leading to severe wind gust. In this case a mesonet station recorded a 79 mph wind wind gust.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: West Texas mesonet site Palo Duro Reservoir |            1 NW. Heat burst suspected with temperature |            increase of 10 degrees and dew point |            temperature decrease of 13 degrees in a 5 |            minute period.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The dry pattern finally changed to allow for several sea breeze showers and storms to develop ahead of a trough of tropical low pressure in the northwestern Gulf of Mexico. A few of these storms produced damaging winds and one storm produced a funnel cloud near La Joya on the evening of August 11th. Additional storms developed August 12th across more of the Rio Grande Valley/Deep South Texas region.  One storm became severe and produced damaging winds of 65 mph near the Mid Valley Airport in Weslaco.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A strong storm developed in southern Hidalgo County and sagged to the southwest the evening of August 11th. At 7:08PM CDT, a member of the public began a Facebook Live that showed a funnel cloud dropping out of the storm. Radar analysis showed some mid-level rotation with the storm to corroborate the video and its timing. It dissipated by the end of the 2 minutes video, so around 7:10PM CDT.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Parts of South Central Texas received above normal rainfall in November including the northern Hill Country, the northern part of the I-35 corridor, and the Coastal Plains. Gonzales County went from D3 to Severe (D2) drought. Blanco and Kendall Counties went from D3 to D4 and Bandera, Gillespie, and Kerr went from D2 to D3. Lake Amistad rose 0.8 feet, but will still 36.2 feet below normal. Lake Travis also rose 0.3 feet, but was 40.3 feet below normal. Medina Lake dropped 0.8 feet and was 78.8 feet below normal. Most public water systems encouraged at least voluntary water restrictions and many had mandatory restrictions in effect. Some the larger services had the following: New Braunfels Stage 1, San Antonio Stage 2, Austin Stage 1, and Kerrville Stage 1.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level storm system became nearly stationary, centered close to El Paso, which allowed extremely moist air to continue to be pumped up into West Texas on the 31st. The near record moisture levels, along with the nearby upper level low, and weak daytime heating, initiated a round of westward-moving showers and thunderstorms that dumped torrential rain in spots adding to the already saturated soils. A number of area roadways become inundated with water stopping traffic and causing some vehicles to be washed off the road. In addition to causing flooding in and around Lubbock (Lubbock County), Brownfield (Terry County), and Post (Garza County), a couple of the tropical showers generated brief funnel clouds. These tropical-type funnels did no known damage.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Photographs on social media showed that a portion of US Highway 87 near Farm to Market Road 41 was flooded.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe (D2) Drought continued to expand in early August due to lack of significant rainfall, hot to very hot temperatures, along with low relative humidity values each afternoon.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe (D2) Drought entered the northwestern tip of Starr County in early August as the drought continued to worsen across Deep South Texas. It stretched from approximately 12 miles west of the Starr/Zapata County line due southwest to just south of New Falcon, TX. The drought would increase into the western third of the county by the 9th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Extreme (D3) Drought developed across western Zapata County due to lack of rainfall, very hot temperatures, and very low relative humidity in the afternoons. Elsewhere, Severe (D2) Drought expanded into northern Hidalgo County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Extreme (D3) Drought entered southwestern Starr County, near Falcon Lake, on August 9th. Severe (D2) Drought also expanded across western Starr County to Rio Grande City on August 9th.  Abundant rainfall fell across the region as an area of low pressure swirled inland from the Gulf of Mexico the weekend of August 12th, 13th, and 14th and allowed the much of the Severe (D2) drought to exit all by the far southwestern portion of Starr County with the August 16th update.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Parts of South Central Texas received above normal rainfall in November including the northern Hill Country, the northern part of the I-35 corridor, and the Coastal Plains. Most of the rest of the area continued to have below normal rain. This had mixed results on the drought. Guadalupe County went from Exceptional (D4) drought to Extreme (D3) drought. Gonzales County went from D3 to Severe (D2) drought. Blanco and Kendall Counties went from D3 to D4 and Bandera, Gillespie, and Kerr went from D2 to D3. Comal and Hays stayed in D4, Bexar and Medina in D3, and Kinney in D2. Of the counties in D2 or worse drought Bandera, Bexar, and Comal had outdoor burn bans in effect at the end of the month. The 7-day average streamflow at the end of the month was below normal (10%-24%) on the Medina River and much below (<10%) normal on the Guadalupe River. The Edwards Aquifer rose 4.4 feet during the month, but was still 30.3 feet below average. Area reservoirs were below normal conservation pool elevation. Lake Amistad rose 0.8 feet, but will still 36.2 feet below normal. Lake Travis also rose 0.3 feet, but was 40.3 feet below normal. Medina Lake dropped 0.8 feet and was 78.8 feet below normal. Most public water systems encouraged at least voluntary water restrictions and many had mandatory restrictions in effect. Some the larger services had the following: New Braunfels Stage 1, San Antonio Stage 2, Austin Stage 1, and Kerrville Stage 1.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The combined Oklahoma and Texas Panhandles saw an influx of moisture from the Gulf of Mexico on May 1st. This axis of low level moisture followed the Rio Grande before moving north up over west Texas. This created an unstable environment primed for severe thunderstorms from the Midland/Odessa area up through the Texas and Oklahoma Panhandles. Thunderstorms initiated along the New Mexico/Texas state line and moved east to northeast depending on the nature of the storm. Multiple supercells formed in the late afternoon into evening hours. These supercells had plenty of moisture, instability and increasing winds with height that enabled them to become severe with very large hail and damaging winds which exceeded 80 mph in some cases.
Severe (D2) Drought continued to expand in early August due to lack of significant rainfall, hot to very hot temperatures, along with low relative humidity values each afternoon.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe (D2) Drought expanded to include northwestern Brooks County. The eastern extent was US-281 from just west of Falfurrias to approximately 10 miles north of Encino before dipping southwest to the Jim Hogg County approximately 11 miles north of the Starr/Jim Hogg/Brooks County lines. On August 9th, Severe (D2) Drought expanded to include all but the southwestern portion of Brooks County. Abundant rainfall fell across the region as an area of low pressure swirled inland from the Gulf of Mexico the weekend of August 12th, 13th, and 14th and allowed drought to exit all of Brooks County with the August 16th update.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A mid to upper level low moved over a warm, moist airmass in South Central Texas and generated slow moving thunderstorms. Some of these storms produced heavy rain that led to flash flooding.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms produced heavy rain that led to flash flooding that closed US 55 south of Camp Wood along the Nueces River. A trained spotter sent pictures of water over the road.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms produced heavy rain that led to flash flooding. ATXFloods reported the low water crossing at the Woodview Mobile Home Park on West Bouldin Creek off Oltorf St. was closed in Austin.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A moisture-rich monsoon fetch, infused by tropical moisture from a wave that moved off the Gulf of Mexico and through South Texas, brought significant amounts of moisture into West Texas. The approach of an upper level storm system well to our north and northwest caused the fetch of monsoon moisture to bend squarely over West Texas. In addition to embedded disturbances within the monsoon, a couple of weak frontal boundaries moved southward into the region. Working together, the moisture, mid-level disturbances, and low-level boundaries generated widespread showers and thunderstorms. The increasingly tropical airmass led to very efficient rain rates and locally heavy rainfall through the evening and overnight hours from the 20th into the 21st.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Texas Department of Transportation reported that a portion of Farm to Market Road 597 was closed due to water over the roadway approximately three miles south of Pep. Radar imagery revealed that storms repeatedly trained over northeastern Hockley County for several hours. Although radar reflectivities were not incredibly high during this time, the repeated storms and very efficient rainfall production led to localized flooding.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the afternoon of the 28th, scattered thunderstorms developed over the central and southwestern South Plains within a low level convergence zone from a surface pressure trough. Hot temperatures and well above average moisture levels fueled the development of convection as it slowly moved to the east. These slow moving storms brought severe wind gusts and widespread flooding to parts of Lubbock and Lynn Counties. These severe winds caused damage within the cities of Lubbock (Lubbock County) and Tahoka (Lynn County), primarily snapping power poles and downing trees and fences. The slow moving nature of the storms combined with the abundant moisture in the atmosphere allowed for extremely heavy rainfall over Lynn County. Several underpasses were flooded along US Highway 87 along with reports of water over the roadway between Tahoka and the Lubbock/Lynn County line.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A thunderstorm that moved over central Lubbock County produced widespread damage across the central portion of the city of Lubbock. Multiple power poles were snapped along with downed trees and fences. At the same time, a wind gust to 58 mph was reported by a Texas Tech University West Texas mesonet site near New Deal at 1635 CST.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The most significant improvement to long term drought conditions for the duration of this drought occurred during the month of August. The greatest improvements were seen over the Rolling Plains and extreme southwestern Texas Panhandle where exceptional drought (D4) was lowered two categories to severe drought (D2). Improvements elsewhere included a reduction to extreme drought (D3) over the southern South Plains and moderate drought (D1) across the northwest South Plains.||This improvement was fueled by widespread rain showers and thunderstorms during the second half of the month. August began hot and dry similar to conditions earlier in the summer, but August trended cooler and more unsettled with periodic bouts of precipitation with flooding at times. This pattern shift occurred following an early departure of a subtropical ridge that typically resides near West Texas in August. As a result,  monsoonal moisture was able to expand east from the desert southwest and combine with occasional weak fronts and disturbances for widespread beneficial rainfall. Rainfall was mostly between 150 and 200 percent of normal with several swaths of 300 percent or more. The improved soil moisture along with increased cloud cover served to keep temperatures near normal for the month following the record breaking heat earlier this summer. Despite the widespread rainfall, negative agricultural impacts continued across the region as a result of long term drought conditions. Fire weather conditions have generally remained low due to relatively light winds and improved moisture. Fuel states significantly improved due to the widespread rainfall during the second half of August.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Beneficial rains have remained isolated across the combined Oklahoma and Texas Panhandles through the month of August. Many areas across the combined Panhandles continued to remain in quite the deficit for rainfall with soil conditions remaining poor to very poor. Some areas did see an improvement with August rains but this was limited to the central to east-central Texas Panhandle. Drought conditions continued to keep rangelands bare, forcing ranchers to continue to sell off cattle as supplemental feeding has been too expensive this year especially when cattle should be grazing. Peanut farmers are expected to see a yield loss of 30% to 50% across much of West Texas into the Panhandle.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The vast majority of Donley County started August off in Severe Drought (D2) with the exception of the northwest corner which was in Moderate Drought (D1) and the very far southwest corner in Extreme Drought (D3). Over the course of the month much of the county received 2 to 6 of rain.  The northwest corner improved to Abnormally Dry (D0) conditions while the central to northeastern portions improved to D1. The far southern third of the county remained in Severe Drought (D2) with the far southwest corner improving to D2. The southern portion of the county remained in D2 with a 6 to 10 deficit year to date.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level system over northern California ushered mid-level moisture into West Texas, with a weak disturbance aloft assisting in shower and thunderstorm development across the Texas and Oklahoma Panhandles. A dryline stretched southwest to northeast across the central Texas Panhandle with strong to severe scattered thunderstorms initiating along and east of the dryline during the late afternoon hours. Large hail up to tennis ball size and wind gusts up to 60 to 70 mph with some areas of blowing dust were reported throughout the late afternoon and early evening hours. By sunset, the storms became linear and wind driven with a decreasing threat of hail but a continuation of severe wind gusts up to 70 to 80 mph. The highest wind gust of 81 mph was measured at the West Texas Mesonet 2 miles east of Pampa, Texas. Following the line of storms, light rain showers developed with bursts of gusty winds across portions of the eastern half of the Texas and Oklahoma Panhandles. In addition, a few non-thunderstorm severe wind gusts also occurred on the western edge of the light precipitation prior to all severe wind reports ending before Midnight.

Severe (D2) drought conditions redeveloped in early August across Nacogdoches and Shelby Counties in Deep East Texas, in response to very hot and dry conditions that developed throughout much of July. The total rainfall amounts across these areas ranged from 1-2 inches throughout July, which was less than 50% below normal. Coupled with the much above normal temperatures observed throughout the month, flash drought conditions redeveloped and persisted through the third week of the month before areas of heavy rain developed, resulting in widespread rainfall amounts of 4-8 inches falling. This eliminated the drought conditions by month's end, with normal streamflow returning across area creeks, streams, and rivers.

Upper ridging was anchored from the Texas and Oklahoma Panhandles southeast into the Lower Mississippi Valley on August 15th-16th, which resulted in very hot and humid conditions across much of the Four State Region allowing for afternoon temperatures to climb into the upper 90s to lower 100s. Very little mixing of dew points was noted across portions of extreme Northeast Texas through this period, with resultant heat indices ranging from 105-108 degrees both days. The passage of a weak surface front on the 17th resulted in slightly cooler conditions, and focused scattered showers and thunderstorms across the area.

An inverted upper trough extending from Central Louisiana into Deep East Texas became absorbed into a weak shear axis across Northeast Louisiana and East Texas on August 5th. These upper level features tapped into a very hot, moist, and unstable air mass with the aid of diurnal heating, with widely scattered showers and thunderstorms developing across East Texas and North Louisiana. Given the elevated nature of these storms, damaging downbursts resulted across the cities of Longview and Mount Pleasant, resulting in numerous trees and power lines downed with some damage to buildings before the storms diminished during the evening.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Widespread wind damage was reported across the city of Mount Pleasant. Trees and power lines were downed on Happy Street and near the intersection of Highway 67 and FM 1402. Winds damaged the doors on a building on Madison Street in Downtown Mount Pleasant.

Approximately 15 trees were snapped and around 30 trees were uprooted at this location. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The combination of deep tropical moisture and a weak stalled frontal boundary led to scattered showers and thunderstorms across the southern Texas Panhandle initially, with activity spreading north through the afternoon and evening.  There was moderate instability, but extremely weak wind shear present in the atmosphere and storms were disorganized, pulsy in nature.  The strongest storms occurred where outflow boundaries collided in the late afternoon and evening.  One strong boundary collision just east of Dumas, Texas led to an unusually strong and long-lived landspout that developed on the northern edge of a thunderstorm, which was generated by the boundary collision.  The landspout moved nearly due north and was on the ground for around 6 minutes and just shy of 2 miles.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The landspout tornado damaged some out buildings and ripped half the roof off an older mobile home which was one of the main damage indicators for this event. Several empty semi tractor trailers at a trucking company were flipped and pushed several yards. Toward the end of the damage path, the tornado destroyed a poorly constructed and old cabin/storage building. Power lines along the path were not damaged and a mobile home directly adjacent to the poorly constructed destroyed building only showed very minor damage. These factors suggest a high end EF0 rating with maximum winds around 85 mph. This survey utilized pictures and information provided by Moore County Emergency management. The landspout was well documented on video by numerous witnesses.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Upper ridging over the Texas and Oklahoma Panhandles that extended east into the Mississippi Valley through much of the summer, finally retreated back west on August 17th, ahead of a weak upper trough that dug southeast into the Four State Region. This trough reinforced a stationary front south into East Texas and North Louisiana during the afternoon, with these features providing the necessary forcing for the development of scattered showers and thunderstorms. Available moisture and very strong heating during the afternoon contributed to very unstable conditions across these areas as temperatures climbed into the lower 100s, resulting in isolated severe thunderstorms developing over Wood County in East Texas. These storms produced damaging winds which downed trees as well as large hail throughout the county before weakening during the evening.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Quarter size hail fell in Quitman.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weak upper trough drifted south into East Texas and North Louisiana on August 10th, and provided enough large scale forcing for scattered showers and thunderstorms during peak heating. Available moisture interacting with afternoon temperatures climbing to near 100 degrees resulted in a very unstable air mass, such that an isolated severe thunderstorm developed over the city of Troup in Southern Smith County, producing damaging winds which damaged a metal roof on a building.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A large metal building suffered roof damage as a result of a microburst from a collapsing thunderstorm.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper trough pulled up stationary across Northeast Texas, extreme Southern Arkansas and North Louisiana during the morning of August 18th, which reinforced a weak surface front south into Deep East Texas and Central Louisiana. This front focused an area of low level moisture pooling across these areas, as well as increased large scale forcing as it tapped into strong heating during the afternoon. Weak steering currents were noted aloft, resulting in an area of slow moving thunderstorms developing across Southern Cherokee and much of Angelina Counties in Deep East Texas, with widespread rainfall amounts of two to four inches falling across these areas in a short period of time. Thus, flash flooding was observed in Downtown Lufkin in Angelina County where a couple of roads were covered in high water.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The intersection of Jefferson Avenue and Raguet Street in Downtown Lufkin was flooded.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level system over northern California ushered mid-level moisture into West Texas, with a weak disturbance aloft assisting in shower and thunderstorm development across the Texas and Oklahoma Panhandles. A dryline stretched southwest to northeast across the central Texas Panhandle with strong to severe scattered thunderstorms initiating along and east of the dryline during the late afternoon hours. Large hail up to tennis ball size and wind gusts up to 60 to 70 mph with some areas of blowing dust were reported throughout the late afternoon and early evening hours. By sunset, the storms became linear and wind driven with a decreasing threat of hail but a continuation of severe wind gusts up to 70 to 80 mph. The highest wind gust of 81 mph was measured at the West Texas Mesonet 2 miles east of Pampa, Texas. Following the line of storms, light rain showers developed with bursts of gusty winds across portions of the eastern half of the Texas and Oklahoma Panhandles. In addition, a few non-thunderstorm severe wind gusts also occurred on the western edge of the light precipitation prior to all severe wind reports ending before Midnight.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A large upper trough shifted southeast into the Four State Region on August 21st through the 22nd, along the backside of an upper level low pressure system over the Great Lakes. This trough slowed as it entered the region, and interacted with rich Gulf moisture and available heating to help focus scattered to numerous showers and thunderstorms across the area. Given the weak steering currents aloft, these thunderstorms were slow moving and were very efficient rainfall producers, which resulted in flash flooding across several areas in East Texas, where widespread rainfall amounts of three to six inches fell with isolated higher amounts over seven inches.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Flooding forced the closure of North Phillips Spring Road, with several vehicles stranded in the high water.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A slow-moving upper trough combined with a stalling front, and a large swath of tropical moisture, to produce record and near-record rainfall across parts of North Texas late August 21 through August 22. Considerable flooding occurred across Dallas County after upwards of 15 inches of rain fell in some areas. Numerous roads, vehicles, homes, buildings and more were flooded and heavily damaged by this event. Damage assessments indicate over 800 buildings and homes were impacted by flood waters, and many were under insured. Preliminary reports indicated 27 destroyed buildings and nearly 300 with major damage. One fatality was reported during this event when a vehicle was swept off a road by a nearby creek.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A social media video indicated significant flooding near Crockett Street and West 7th Street in Fort Worth, with water depth near the tops of car tires.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A trough of low pressure drifted from near the Louisiana Coast on August 12th to the Middle Texas coast by early on the 14th.  The trough, which included a mid-level circulation, moved across the coast near Riviera and would continue through Laredo between the 14th and 15th before moving northwest along the Rio Grande toward the Texas Big Bend region later on the 15th and 16th. ||Welcome rainfall of 3 to 7 inches during the day on the 14th helped quench the drought across the ranch country, and a small area from central Cameron county to southeast Willacy County also received an estimated 3 to 6 or more inches of rain. A torrential band may have dropped more than 8 inches along U.S. 83 in extreme northwest Zapata County late on August 15th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Torrential rainfall, with local estimates of 2 or more inches per hour for two hours, produced street flooding from San Benito through La Tina Ranch, including along city and rural roads, with 1 to 2 feet of water on roads where the heaviest rainfall fell.  There were no reports of flooding of structures in these areas, and flood receded quickly after the slow moving band ended.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A large upper low pressure system moved into the Great Lakes region on August 22nd, with a trailing upper trough extending southwest of this low into the Southern Plains. This trough induced surface low development along a weak surface boundary across North Texas, and focused areas of showers and embedded thunderstorms over much of the Four State Region. Weak surface heating near this boundary contributed to modestly unstable conditions within a moist environment in place, with enough low level shear available which resulted in a low topped supercell developing near Winona in Northeast Smith County Texas. This storm produced a brief EF-1 tornado which just missed the Winona Independent School District campus, but still downed numerous trees along its path before lifting.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An EF-1 tornado with estimated maximum winds near 95 mph touched down just south of County Road 345 on the west side of Winona. There, it lofted a small metal outbuilding, throwing it across the road, while also uprooting a tree. It continued on to clip the Winona Independent School District campus, where it lifted a training sled as it crossed the football field and damaged the roof of a dugout. The tornado just missed hitting the school buildings by only around 200 yards. The tornado continued on to hit another small metal outbuilding, rolling and destroying it before crossing FM 16. The tornado then paralleled Hussey Circle, downing several more large branches and snapping a large tree which fell into a home. Additional hardwood trees were uprooted as it crossed County Road 155, where the tornado reached its widest point before lifting shortly thereafter.

While these hot conditions were again observed on the 4th, greater mixing of dew points correlated to slightly lower heat indices below 105 degrees across East Texas.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level system over northern California ushered mid-level moisture into West Texas, with a weak disturbance aloft assisting in shower and thunderstorm development across the Texas and Oklahoma Panhandles. A dryline stretched southwest to northeast across the central Texas Panhandle with strong to severe scattered thunderstorms initiating along and east of the dryline during the late afternoon hours. Large hail up to tennis ball size and wind gusts up to 60 to 70 mph with some areas of blowing dust were reported throughout the late afternoon and early evening hours. By sunset, the storms became linear and wind driven with a decreasing threat of hail but a continuation of severe wind gusts up to 70 to 80 mph. The highest wind gust of 81 mph was measured at the West Texas Mesonet 2 miles east of Pampa, Texas. Following the line of storms, light rain showers developed with bursts of gusty winds across portions of the eastern half of the Texas and Oklahoma Panhandles. In addition, a few non-thunderstorm severe wind gusts also occurred on the western edge of the light precipitation prior to all severe wind reports ending before Midnight.

Considerable flooding occurred across Dallas County after upwards of 15 inches of rain fell in some areas. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe (D2) drought conditions expanded to include northern Zapata County in late July. Extreme (D3) drought conditions continued in far northwestern Jim Hogg County. The lack of significant rain combined with hot to very hot temperatures and low relative humidity values each afternoon led to the expansion of the drought through July.  Water storage levels at Falcon International Reservoir continued to edge toward levels not seen since 1998-2002.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Extreme (D3) Drought continued in far northwestern Jim Hogg County, including the Jim Hogg County Airport. Severe (D2) Drought continued to include much of the northern part of the county. It stretched from approximately 1.5 miles south of Texas Highway 16 along the Jim Hogg and Zapata County line to 19 miles due south of Hebbronville to the northwestern cutout of Brooks County 2.3 miles south of TX-285.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe (D2) Drought continued to expand in early August due to lack of significant rainfall, hot to very hot temperatures, along with low relative humidity values each afternoon.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe (D2) Drought expanded to include all of Zapata County on August 2nd as the lack of rain began leading to water conservation efforts in Zapata as Falcon Lake dipped to its lowest levels (Texas share) on record and the lowest since 2002 for combined U.S. and Mexico water storage levels.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Beneficial rains have remained isolated across the combined Oklahoma and Texas Panhandles through the month of August. Many areas across the combined Panhandles continued to remain in quite the deficit for rainfall with soil conditions remaining poor to very poor. Some areas did see an improvement with August rains but this was limited to the central to east-central Texas Panhandle. Drought conditions continued to keep rangelands bare, forcing ranchers to continue to sell off cattle as supplemental feeding has been too expensive this year especially when cattle should be grazing. Peanut farmers are expected to see a yield loss of 30% to 50% across much of West Texas into the Panhandle.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Gray County started the month of August with the far southeast corner of the county in Severe Drought (D2) while the rest of the county was in Moderate Drought (D1). Within the first week the county received enough rain for the area of D2 to improve to D1 as well as areas in D1 across central portions of the county to improve to D0 (Abnormally Dry).  With 3 to 5 of rainfall across the county by the end of the month the vast majority of the county improved to D0, with the exception of a small area in the northwest and southeast that remained in D1.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe (D2) to Extreme (D3) drought conditions continued across portions of East Texas through late August. This was in response to a flash drought that resulted from an exceptionally hot and dry month in June with well below normal rainfall in what is historically one of the wettest months on average. This was then followed by an even hotter and largely dry month in July. The total rainfall amounts were generally around an inch or less in June, which was only near 25% of normal. Near to slightly above normal rainfall returned in August, and while this did improve drought conditions across much of East Texas, moderate drought persisted across Red River County as well as the western sections of East Texas to end the month. This dryness contributed to lower than normal streamflow observed across area creeks, streams, and rivers before improving by late month.

An upper level system over northern California ushered mid-level moisture into West Texas, with a weak disturbance aloft assisting in shower and thunderstorm development across the Texas and Oklahoma Panhandles. A dryline stretched southwest to northeast across the central Texas Panhandle with strong to severe scattered thunderstorms initiating along and east of the dryline during the late afternoon hours. Large hail up to tennis ball size and wind gusts up to 60 to 70 mph with some areas of blowing dust were reported throughout the late afternoon and early evening hours. By sunset, the storms became linear and wind driven with a decreasing threat of hail but a continuation of severe wind gusts up to 70 to 80 mph. The highest wind gust of 81 mph was measured at the West Texas Mesonet 2 miles east of Pampa, Texas. Following the line of storms, light rain showers developed with bursts of gusty winds across portions of the eastern half of the Texas and Oklahoma Panhandles. In addition, a few non-thunderstorm severe wind gusts also occurred on the western edge of the light precipitation prior to all severe wind reports ending before Midnight.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: There was a report receivd of a metal barn destroyed.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Extreme (D3) Drought developed across western Zapata County due to lack of rainfall, very hot temperatures, and very low relative humidity in the afternoons. Elsewhere, Severe (D2) Drought expanded into northern Hidalgo County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Lack of rainfall, very hot temperatures, and low relative humidity in the afternoons led to the development of Extreme (D3) drought in the western two thirds of Zapata County. Rainfall on August 14th and 15th allowed the northern portion of the Extreme (D3) drought to be downgraded to Severe (D2) Drought, and trim the area of Severe (D2) Drought to all but the eastern fifth of the county on the 16th. Reservoir levels at Falcon reached the lowest levels (Texas share) on record between the 13th and 15th, and were at their lowest levels since 2002 during this time.  Torrential rains of 6 to more than 8 inches late on the 15th over and just north of the lake along the Rio Grande would bring a flood wave into the reservoir, starting a rise that would bring water storage levels above the new Texas share record and similar total share values from 2002.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The dry pattern finally changed to allow for several sea breeze showers and storms to develop ahead of a trough of tropical low pressure in the northwestern Gulf of Mexico. A few of these storms produced damaging winds and one storm produced a funnel cloud near La Joya on the evening of August 11th. Additional storms developed August 12th across more of the Rio Grande Valley/Deep South Texas region.  One storm became severe and produced damaging winds of 65 mph near the Mid Valley Airport in Weslaco.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A pulse-severe thunderstorm produced a microburst with winds estimated at 65 mph across the northeast side of Weslaco.  Along its 2.3 mile track, damage included blown in siding at hangars at the airportand peeled back a metal roof on one of them.  Other damage included a small outbuilding that was flipped over, bent in fences, and a trampoline lifted and flung. The Mid Valley Airport ASOS in Weslaco officially recorded a 56 mph wind gust, but missed the core being about 300 meters west of the downburst.

Despite only being around a 1 to 2 deficit for the month, much of the county remained in a 2 to 4 deficit over the last three months.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Beneficial rains have remained isolated across the combined Oklahoma and Texas Panhandles through the month of August. Many areas across the combined Panhandles continued to remain in quite the deficit for rainfall with soil conditions remaining poor to very poor. Some areas did see an improvement with August rains but this was limited to the central to east-central Texas Panhandle. Drought conditions continued to keep rangelands bare, forcing ranchers to continue to sell off cattle as supplemental feeding has been too expensive this year especially when cattle should be grazing. Peanut farmers are expected to see a yield loss of 30% to 50% across much of West Texas into the Panhandle.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Around a third of the county in the west central to northwest portion of the county started the month in Severe Drought (D2), while the rest of the county was in Moderate Drought (D1). The county ended the this month plus the last two months with a 3 month deficit around 2 to 6. The area of D2 expanded to cover much of the western half of the county.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level system over northern California ushered mid-level moisture into West Texas, with a weak disturbance aloft assisting in shower and thunderstorm development across the Texas and Oklahoma Panhandles. A dryline stretched southwest to northeast across the central Texas Panhandle with strong to severe scattered thunderstorms initiating along and east of the dryline during the late afternoon hours. Large hail up to tennis ball size and wind gusts up to 60 to 70 mph with some areas of blowing dust were reported throughout the late afternoon and early evening hours. By sunset, the storms became linear and wind driven with a decreasing threat of hail but a continuation of severe wind gusts up to 70 to 80 mph. The highest wind gust of 81 mph was measured at the West Texas Mesonet 2 miles east of Pampa, Texas. Following the line of storms, light rain showers developed with bursts of gusty winds across portions of the eastern half of the Texas and Oklahoma Panhandles. In addition, a few non-thunderstorm severe wind gusts also occurred on the western edge of the light precipitation prior to all severe wind reports ending before Midnight.

Severe (D2) to Extreme (D3) drought conditions continued across portions of East Texas through late August. This was in response to a flash drought that resulted from an exceptionally hot and dry month in June with well below normal rainfall in what is historically one of the wettest months on average. This was then followed by an even hotter and largely dry month in July. The total rainfall amounts were generally around an inch or less in June, which was only near 25% of normal. Near to slightly above normal rainfall returned in August, and while this did improve drought conditions across much of East Texas, moderate drought persisted across Red River County as well as the western sections of East Texas to end the month. This dryness contributed to lower than normal streamflow observed across area creeks, streams, and rivers before improving by late month.

A slow-moving upper trough combined with a stalling front, and a large swath of tropical moisture, to produce record and near-record rainfall across parts of North Texas late August 21 through August 22. Considerable flooding occurred across Dallas County after upwards of 15 inches of rain fell in some areas. Numerous roads, vehicles, homes, buildings and more were flooded and heavily damaged by this event. Damage assessments indicate over 800 buildings and homes were impacted by flood waters, and many were under insured. Preliminary reports indicated 27 destroyed buildings and nearly 300 with major damage. One fatality was reported during this event when a vehicle was swept off a road by a nearby creek.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Trinity River in Fort Worth rose out of its bank and over Forest Park Rd from I-30 to Weatherford Road.

Considerable flooding occurred across Dallas County after upwards of 15 inches of rain fell in some areas. Numerous roads, vehicles, homes, buildings and more were flooded and heavily damaged by this event. Damage assessments indicate over 800 buildings and homes were impacted by flood waters, and many were under insured. Preliminary reports indicated 27 destroyed buildings and nearly 300 with major damage. One fatality was reported during this event when a vehicle was swept off a road by a nearby creek.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Spence Road, and Gin Road near Walker Creek Road were all closed due to high water.

This led to an improvement in conditions with the southwest two-thirds ending the month in D2 and the northeastern third ending the month in Moderate Drought (D1). Much of the southern half of the county remained in a 6 to 12 deficit year to date.

By sunset, the storms became linear and wind driven with a decreasing threat of hail but a continuation of severe wind gusts up to 70 to 80 mph. The highest wind gust of 81 mph was measured at the West Texas Mesonet 2 miles east of Pampa, Texas. Following the line of storms, light rain showers developed with bursts of gusty winds across portions of the eastern half of the Texas and Oklahoma Panhandles. In addition, a few non-thunderstorm severe wind gusts also occurred on the western edge of the light precipitation prior to all severe wind reports ending before Midnight.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weak upper trough shifted southeast into the Red River Valley of Southern Oklahoma and Western Arkansas during the morning of August 9th, which focused concentrated areas of showers and thunderstorms as it encountered a hot, very moist, and unstable air mass. These showers and thunderstorms were slow moving, with widespread 2-4+ inches of rain falling over both the Texas and Arkansas sides of Texarkana, as well as across much of Southwest Arkansas. This resulted in flash flooding across the city of Texarkana, with numerous roads flooded as 3.94 inches of rain fell over the course of a few hours at the Texarkana Regional Airport.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous roads were flooded across both the Texas and Arkansas sides of Texarkana.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms formed on the higher terrain of eastern New Mexico on the afternoon of the 12th. A few of these storms moved into the extreme southwestern Texas Panhandle during the evening hours where instability was sufficient to sustain convective development. These storms were able to produce a severe wind gust near Dimmitt (Castro County).
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A Texas Tech University West Texas mesonet site near Dimmitt measured a wind gust of 64 mph. Additionally, an NWS cooperative weather observer reported that a portable toilet was blown over.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Rainfall deficits continued to deepen throughout July as heat ramped up due to the lack of moisture. Extreme drought (D3) conditions grew to include all but portions of the western South Plains where earlier spring rains were limiting drought conditions to severe (D2) levels. Exceptional drought (D4) expanded slightly to encompass portions of the northern and southern South Plains, Rolling Plains, and extreme southwestern Texas Panhandle.||Rainfall through the month was between zero and 50 percent of normal. Additionally, this July was the warmest on record for several locations including Lubbock (Lubbock County) where 18 days of 100 degrees or higher temperatures were recorded which is a new record. The North American monsoon remained mostly to the west of the region which is typical for July. This monsoon moisture expanded into West Texas for a few days during the month which brought beneficial but spotty rainfall. Wide ranging agricultural impacts continued with overall dry conditions resulting in a difficult year for cotton growth. Despite the dryness, relatively light winds mitigated wildfire danger.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the month of July some areas, especially in the western combined Panhandles improved while other areas saw degradations in categorical drought per the US Drought Monitor. Overall drought conditions persisted across the combined Panhandles during the month of July. Irrigated corn was doing well but well behind schedule. Winter wheat harvest ended with yields well below normal. Rangeland and pasture conditions  continued to be poor with an increase in cattle continuing to be sold, well above past years, as supplemental feeding becomes expensive when cattle should be grazing natural grasslands. A couple of wildfires in the Texas occurred during the month of July due to the drought conditions as well.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A small area in the far southern portion of the county was in Severe Drought (D2) at the beginning of the month. The majority of the county was in Moderate Drought (D1) with a small area in the far northern portion of the county was only abnormally dry (D0). A few isolated areas of the county received just above 2 of rain for the month, while the rest of the county only received 0.5 to 1.5 of rain.  With this still being between 1 and 2 below normal especially in the southern half of the county degradation were observed in drought conditions by the end of the month. The county ended with the far southwest corner in Extreme Drought (D3) and the rest of the county in Severe Drought (D2).

A relatively dry sub-cloud layer allowed a couple of these storms to produce severe downburst winds in Lubbock (Lubbock County) and near Turkey (Hall County).
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A wind gust of 63 mph was measured at the National Weather Service Weather Forecast Office in Lubbock.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Very hot temperatures on the afternoon of the third and an approaching weak mid-level circulation allowed for isolated to scattered thunderstorms to develop off the caprock. Relatively dry sub-cloud layers allowed for strong downburst winds to develop which produced a couple of severe wind gusts near Hackberry (Cottle County) and near Silverton (Briscoe County).
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A Texas Tech University West Texas mesonet site near Hackberry measured severe wind gusts from 1503 CST through 1504 CST. A peak wind gust of 60 mph was measured at 1504 CST.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Rainfall deficits continued to deepen throughout July as heat ramped up due to the lack of moisture. Extreme drought (D3) conditions grew to include all but portions of the western South Plains where earlier spring rains were limiting drought conditions to severe (D2) levels. Exceptional drought (D4) expanded slightly to encompass portions of the northern and southern South Plains, Rolling Plains, and extreme southwestern Texas Panhandle.||Rainfall through the month was between zero and 50 percent of normal. Additionally, this July was the warmest on record for several locations including Lubbock (Lubbock County) where 18 days of 100 degrees or higher temperatures were recorded which is a new record. The North American monsoon remained mostly to the west of the region which is typical for July. This monsoon moisture expanded into West Texas for a few days during the month which brought beneficial but spotty rainfall. Wide ranging agricultural impacts continued with overall dry conditions resulting in a difficult year for cotton growth. Despite the dryness, relatively light winds mitigated wildfire danger.

The combination of a strong area of high pressure across the Mid-South and a coastal trough that developed into a coastal low led to widespread beach erosion and minor coastal flooding along South Padre Island the weekend of November 19th through November 21st. Residual swells led to minor beach erosion through November 24th. Winds gusting to 45 knots created wave heights at Buoy 42020 of nearly 20 feet the evening of November 19th. The long duration of the northeasterly winds led to multiple rounds of coastal flooding starting November 19th and continued through November 24th. This resulted in the County Beach Access Points being closed for several days along with water reaching Highway 100 on South Padre Island and overtopping Highway 4 near SpaceX and Boca Chica Beach.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A 2.1-foot storm tide, as observed by NOAA's National Ocean Service site at Port Isabel (PTIT2), affected Coastal Cameron County from November 18th through very early in the morning on November 21st. The storm tide remained between 1.25-foot and 2.1-foot the entire time. A picture from social media also showed water overtopping Highway 4 out to Boca Chica Beach the morning of November 20th when the storm tide was running between 1.8-foot and 2.0-foot.

During the month of July some areas, especially in the western combined Panhandles improved while other areas saw degradations in categorical drought per the US Drought Monitor. Overall drought conditions persisted across the combined Panhandles during the month of July. Irrigated corn was doing well but well behind schedule. Winter wheat harvest ended with yields well below normal. Rangeland and pasture conditions  continued to be poor with an increase in cattle continuing to be sold, well above past years, as supplemental feeding becomes expensive when cattle should be grazing natural grasslands. A couple of wildfires in the Texas occurred during the month of July due to the drought conditions as well.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Gray County was only abnormally dry (D0) at the beginning of the month. July was abnormally dry with Moderate Drought (D1) returning by mid week. By the third week 75% of the county slipped into Severe Drought (D2).  It wasn't till a decent rain event during the last few days of the month that helped the county end in Moderate Drought with the exception of the far southeast corner of the county. The county's overall monthly rain total ended with a large range from 1.5 to 5.

EVENT_NARRATIVE: Wheeler County started the month out with only abnormally dry conditions (D0). However, July was abnormally dry and hot with drought conditions reappearing by mid month. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: High dewpoint temperatures combined with very hot daytime high temperatures on July 20th, resulting in heat index values exceeding 111 degrees in Hidalgo, Starr, and Zapata Counties during the afternoon.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: This event is based largely on observed heat index values across Southern Hidalgo County and Zapata County. Both counties saw heat indices top out above 111 degrees for several hours. Given the higher heat index values in both Hidalgo and Zapata Counties, it is inferred that Starr County also experienced heat indices in excess of 111 degrees for at least two hours. The Falcon Lake RAWS site recorded values technically reaching Excessive Heat criteria, but this observation site has a history of running notably higher than surrounding areas. Additionally, the Texas Mesonet site in La Gloria recorded a heat index of 111 between 3:50PM CDT and 4:20PM CDT. No heat-related injuries or fatalities were reported as of this writing.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe (D2) to Extreme (D3) drought conditions developed across portions of East and Northeast Texas in late July and continued through the end of the month. This was in response to a flash drought that resulted from an exceptionally hot and dry month in June with well below normal rainfall in what is historically one of the wettest months on average. This was then followed by an even hotter and equally dry month in July with the total rainfall amounts for both months generally around an inch or less, which was only near 25% of normal. This dryness contributed to lower than normal streamflow observed across area creeks, streams, and rivers.

Lack of significant rain, hot to very hot temperatures, and low relative humidity combined to allow Extreme (D3) Drought conditions return to the very northern portion of Jim Hogg County on July 19th. Severe (D2) Drought conditions expanded southward to include the northern quarter part of the county.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The very northern part of Jim Hogg County saw Extreme (D3) Drought return in mid-July. This includes the northern half of the town of Hebbronville. Severe (D2) Drought also expanded southward in mid-July.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: After having missed the heaviest rain at the end of May, Severe (D2) Drought continued for the northern tip of Jim Hogg County, including most of Hebbronville, to start July.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The very northern part of Jim Hogg County, which missed out on the heavier rain events in late May, saw Severe (D2) Drought return in mid-June and continue through the month of July. This includes area northwest of the Hebbronville Border Patrol Station and does include much of the town of Hebbronville.

A strong upper level low pressure system shifted northeast out of the Central Rockies across Eastern Colorado and Northwest Kansas during the day on December 13th, which allowed for surface low pressure to develop along an attendant cold front that extended south across Western Kansas into Western Oklahoma and Northwest Texas. Meanwhile, a tightening pressure gradient ahead of the front resulted in strong southerly low level winds across the Southern Plains and Lower Mississippi Valley, with an increase in warmer, more humid and unstable air spreading back north into East Texas and the Lower Mississippi Valley. Large scale forcing increased during the afternoon across East Texas ahead of the approaching upper trough, along a dry line that had mixed east ahead of the cold front. Thus, scattered showers and thunderstorms developed across much of East Texas, some of which became severe as they tapped the strongly sheared air mass in place and the better instability contributed from daytime heating. EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several trees were downed and mobile home covers were damaged along CR 317 just south of FM 16. Fences and telephone poles were also snapped.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong and persistent upper-level ridge across the Four Corners Region retrograded slightly westward, allowing an upper-level trough to shift southward from the Plains and Ozarks. The trough helped to drive a weak frontal boundary in the region where ample instability was in place as daytime maximum temperatures averaged between 100-105 degrees on July 13th. Convection began to form by mid to late afternoon with several thunderstorms quickly becoming severe in the very unstable conditions. The high-based thunderstorms presented a primary damaging wind threat, which resulted in numerous damage reports through the afternoon and evening hours on the 13th. Some of the severe thunderstorms also produced hail of various sizes, including a few reports of large hail. These storms continued through the early morning hours of the 14th before diminishing. Additional isolated severe thunderstorms developed during the afternoon of the 14th over Eastern Smith County, producing damaging winds that tore a portion of the roof off of the Chapel Hill High School cafeteria.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Texas Electric Cooperative reported several power line poles downed near Crystal Lake on the west side of Joaquin.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Conditions were favorable for wildfire spread in the days following the July 4th holiday thanks to hot temperatures, low relative humidity and breezy conditions behind the sea breeze each afternoon. These moderate to strong easterly winds behind the sea breeze allowed for rapid wildfire spread in a short amount of time each evening and two fires rapidly spread: The Deer Wildfire in Kenedy County on July 6th and the Blanket Wildfire in Brooks County on July 9th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The event known as the Deer Wildfire was estimated to have initiated around 1:21PM CDT about 9 miles northwest of Armstrong, TX, on or near the Encino Division of the King Ranch. It burned until July 9th when it was announced to be 100 percent contained at 9:52AM CDT. This wildfire consumed 1,062 acres. A Spot Request submitted by the Texas A&M Forest Service was used as a guide for the ignition time and rapid spread that followed.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A fast-moving cold front served as a focus for thunderstorm development across North and Central Texas, as an upper level storm system swept across the Plains the afternoon of November 4. Large hail and damaging wind gusts accompanied several of these storms, and a total of 5 tornadoes occurred. The hardest-hit area was Lamar County, where an EF-4 tornado occurred.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tornado formed near Brookston in western Lamar County and tracked rapidly northeastward, passing to the northwest of Paris, Texas before exiting the northern edge of Lamar County, east of Arthur City. The tornado continued into Choctaw County Oklahoma and additional information about the damage in that county can be found in a separate entry. Several dozen individual homes, businesses and outbuildings were impacted across western and northern Lamar County.  Damage consistent with EF-3 intensity tornadic winds of 150-160 mph were identified at several locations west through north of Paris.  In particular, several residences along Farm Market Road 1499 northwest of Paris were completely unroofed, with most external and internal walls destroyed.  This damage was consistent with tornado intensities of approximately 160 mph. One particular house on CR 33620 revealed EF-4 damage, with estimated winds of at least 170 MPH. EF-3 damage of 145 to 155 mph was also identified with a small number of structures along Farm to Market Road 906 near Mideity, as well as with a residence along Farm to Market Road 2820 west-northwest of Paris.  Primary damage to these structures was the total loss of roofs and large-scale interior and exterior wall failure. EF-2 damage, consistent with winds of 111 to 135 mph, was identified with a number of other structures along the tornado's path.  Structures with this degree of damage had either all or large portions of their roofs destroyed or significantly damaged, with some wall failures.  Widespread EF-1 damage was also apparent all along the track from Brookston to east of Arthur City, as evidenced by trees uprooted, power poles snapped, outbuildings severely damaged, and/or wood frame homes with serious roof damage. Maximum estimated winds were 170 mph.

A strong and persistent upper-level ridge across the Four Corners Region retrograded slightly westward, allowing an upper-level trough to shift southward from the Plains and Ozarks. The trough helped to drive a weak frontal boundary in the region where ample instability was in place as daytime maximum temperatures averaged between 100-105 degrees on July 13th. Convection began to form by mid to late afternoon with several thunderstorms quickly becoming severe in the very unstable conditions. The high-based thunderstorms presented a primary damaging wind threat, which resulted in numerous damage reports through the afternoon and evening hours on the 13th. Some of the severe thunderstorms also produced hail of various sizes, including a few reports of large hail. These storms continued through the early morning hours of the 14th before diminishing. Additional isolated severe thunderstorms developed during the afternoon of the 14th over Eastern Smith County, producing damaging winds that tore a portion of the roof off of the Chapel Hill High School cafeteria.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Widespread downed trees, power lines, and power poles reported throughout the city of Tyler.

Elevated longshore and rip currents at local beaches on the afternoon and evening of July 2nd contributed to a drowning and one successful rescue on South Padre Island. A slight southeasterly swell was noted at offshore buoys along with eyewitness accounts from those in the surf that weekend. Cameron County Beach Patrol responded to a call regarding two victims on the evening of July 2nd, with Beach Patrol suggesting the fatality was current-related.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Cameron County Beach Patrol responded to a call regarding two possible drowning victims, which came in around 7:10PM CDT on July 2nd. Witnesses suggested the fatality was rip/longshore current related, and an off-duty NWS employee vouched for the dangerous rip current/longshore current potential during the entire weekend (July 2-4).  ||A 37-year old tourist swimming in the Gulf of Mexico off South Padre Island, about 2.5 miles north of Cameron County Beach Access #5, drowned in the current. A child, age unknown, was also rescued from the water by bystanders before the Beach Patrol arrived.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Severe (D2) Drought conditions expanded to include northern Zapata County in late July. The lack of significant rain combined with hot to very hot temperatures and low relative humidity values each afternoon led to the expansion of the drought.  Reservoir levels at Falcon Lake fell toward 30-year low values, to levels not seen since between 1998 and 2002.  The levels would continue to drop into mid August.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Severe (D2) Drought expanded to include much of the northern part of the county. It stretched from approximately 1.5 miles south of Texas Highway 16 along the Jim Hogg and Zapata County border to 19 miles due south of Hebbronville to the northwestern cutout of Brooks County 2.3 miles south of TX-285.

On July 25th, a small grass fire in Balch Springs (Dallas County) destroyed at 9 homes and damaged 17 more.

A strong upper-level ridge set up across the western U.S. with broad ridging extending eastward across the Ark-La-Tex region. However, slight weakening along the eastern extent of the ridge allowed for convection to become more likely with diurnal heating. At the surface, a weak frontal boundary located from along the middle Red River Valley eastward into central Arkansas had become nearly stationary. Along and south of the boundary, plentiful moisture characteristic of dew points mainly in the lower 70s were noted. Some lingering outflow boundaries were also present from earlier convection, and these features combined to help trigger an isolated severe thunderstorm during the early evening hours in Northeastern Panola County. This storm produced isolated damaging wind gusts just west of Bethany.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was downed along Highway 79 near Bethany.

The center of a dominant upper-level ridge retrograded slightly westward over the Rockies, allowing a weak shortwave trough to advance southeast across the Southern Plains into the Ark-La-Tex region. This trough was accompanied by a weak frontal boundary at the surface, moving south from Oklahoma and Arkansas and eventually south of the Red River by late afternoon in the evening hours. Ahead of the boundary, temperatures in the triple digits combined with a very unstable air mass and precipitable water values near two inches. This resulted in elevated thunderstorms developing within the unstable air mass, where isolated damaging wind gusts were produced from a few severe thunderstorms across portions of Northeast Texas during the late afternoon and early evening.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Trees reported down.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The center of a dominant upper-level ridge retrograded slightly westward over the Rockies, allowing a weak shortwave trough to advance southeast across the Southern Plains into the Ark-La-Tex region. This trough was accompanied by a weak frontal boundary at the surface, moving south from Oklahoma and Arkansas and eventually south of the Red River by late afternoon in the evening hours. Ahead of the boundary, temperatures in the triple digits combined with a very unstable air mass and precipitable water values near two inches. This resulted in elevated thunderstorms developing within the unstable air mass, where isolated damaging wind gusts were produced from a few severe thunderstorms across portions of Northeast Texas during the late afternoon and early evening.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Fences and numerous trees reported down.

A strong and persistent upper-level ridge across the Four Corners Region retrograded slightly westward, allowing an upper-level trough to shift southward from the Plains and Ozarks. The trough helped to drive a weak frontal boundary in the region where ample instability was in place as daytime maximum temperatures averaged between 100-105 degrees on July 13th. Convection began to form by mid to late afternoon with several thunderstorms quickly becoming severe in the very unstable conditions. The high-based thunderstorms presented a primary damaging wind threat, which resulted in numerous damage reports through the afternoon and evening hours on the 13th. Some of the severe thunderstorms also produced hail of various sizes, including a few reports of large hail. These storms continued through the early morning hours of the 14th before diminishing. Additional isolated severe thunderstorms developed during the afternoon of the 14th over Eastern Smith County, producing damaging winds that tore a portion of the roof off of the Chapel Hill High School cafeteria.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Nickel sized hail reported in Lone Star.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The central to eastern Oklahoma Panhandle as well as the surrounding areas in the northern Texas Panhandle continued to see a significant lack of soil moisture. Ranchers and farmers continue to struggle from the lack of rainfall. Crop yields came in low, as expected, over the course of September. Herds had been kept lower than previous years in order to reduce the cost of supplemental feeding as pastures remain barren. Unlike in previous years, high winds and low relative humidity days had been almost non-existent in September which kept wildfire activity at bay. Many burn bans were implemented or retained for the driest of areas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The southeastern corner of Ochiltree County received 1.5 to 2.5 inches of rain during the month of September. The rest of the county received less than 1.5 inches with isolated areas only receiving 0.1 to 0.25 inches. Almost the entire county started the month in severe drought (D2) and ended the month in severe drought (D2) with the exception of a very small portion in the far southeast corner that started and ended in moderate drought (D1).

Soil moisture remained short to very short through the month of November. The continuation of extended drought left farmers and ranchers seeking ways to water crops and feed livestock. Drought continued to affect the quality of forage, forcing producers to bale failed crops as well as grasses that are not normally harvested as forage. The worst of the drought in the Great Plains was across the Oklahoma Panhandle and far northern Texas Panhandle into much of southern Kansas and into Oklahoma. A few counties in the Panhandles were free of Severe Drought (D2) for the month of November but were not completely free of drought and were classified in Moderate Drought (D1).
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The northern and western portions of Ochiltree County started the month with Extreme Drought (D3) conditions while the rest of the county to the southeast started the month with Severe Drought (D2)  conditions. The southeast corner of the county received close to 150 percent of normal rainfall for the month while the rest of the county only received 50 to 75 percent of normal rainfall for the month. Because the monthly normal is around 0.75 to 0.8 and the county still remains in a year-to-date rainfall deficit of 4 to 8 leaving drought categories unchanged at the end of November.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: After beneficial rain in August, dry weather returned in September. Most of South Central Texas had below normal precipitation and drought conditions worsened or remained the same. Guadalupe and Hays Counties worsened from Extreme (D3) category to Exceptional (D4) category. Bandera and Caldwell went from Severe (D2) category to D3. Bastrop, Fayette, Lavaca, and Travis worsened to D2. Comal remained in D4. Bexar, Blanco, Kendall, and Medina stayed in D3. Burnet, Gillespie, Gonzales, Kerr, Kinney, Llano, Maverick, Real, Uvalde, Williamson, and Wilson remained in D2. Of the counties in D2 or worse drought Comal, Hays, Bexar, Blanco, Caldwell, Medina, Fayette, Maverick, Travis, and Wilson had outdoor burn bans in effect. At the end of the month the 7-day average streamflow was much below (<10%) normal on the Frio River, below (10%-24%) normal on the Medina River, below normal on the San Antonio River, much below normal on the Guadalupe River, normal to below normal on the upper Colorado River, and much below normal on the lower Colorado. The Edwards Aquifer dropped 3.6 feet and was 32.2 feet below normal at the end of the month. Area reservoirs continued to lose water. Medina Lake was down 1.1 feet to 76.8 feet below conservation pool level, and Lake Travis was down 2.0 feet to 38.2 feet below conservation level. Lake Amistad rose 12.6 feet during the month due to rainfall in Mexico but was still 41.5 feet below conservation level. Most public water systems encouraged at least voluntary water restrictions, and many had mandatory restrictions in effect. Some the larger services had the following: New Braunfels Stage 1, San Antonio Stage 2, Austin Stage 1, and Kerrville Stage 1.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The central to eastern Oklahoma Panhandle as well as the surrounding areas in the northern Texas Panhandle continued to see a significant lack of soil moisture. Ranchers and farmers continue to struggle from the lack of rainfall. Crop yields came in low, as expected, over the course of September. Herds had been kept lower than previous years in order to reduce the cost of supplemental feeding as pastures remain barren. Unlike in previous years, high winds and low relative humidity days had been almost non-existent in September which kept wildfire activity at bay. Many burn bans were implemented or retained for the driest of areas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Moore County started the month of September with the northern third in Severe Drought (D2) and the southern two thirds in Moderate Drought (D1). The county received 0.5 to 2 inches of rain over the course of the month. This rainfall was not enough to improve conditions, thus ending the month in the same drought categories that existed at the start of the month. Moore County remained in a 2 to 6 inch deficit year to date.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Isolated thunderstorms developed along a cold front during the early morning hours of the 4th across central Oklahoma, with a couple severe wind reports received. Storms redeveloped during the afternoon and produced isolated wind and hail across portions of western north Texas.

The central to eastern Oklahoma Panhandle as well as the surrounding areas in the northern Texas Panhandle continued to see a significant lack of soil moisture. Ranchers and farmers continue to struggle from the lack of rainfall. Crop yields came in low, as expected, over the course of September. Herds had been kept lower than previous years in order to reduce the cost of supplemental feeding as pastures remain barren. Unlike in previous years, high winds and low relative humidity days had been almost non-existent in September which kept wildfire activity at bay. Many burn bans were implemented or retained for the driest of areas.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Collingsworth County started the month of September with the far southeast corner of the county in Extreme Drought (D3) and the northwest corner in Moderate Drought (D1) with the majority of area in the central part of the county in Severe Drought (D2). The majority of the county received 1 to 1.5 inch of rainfall while the far southeast corner only received 0.1 to 0.25 inches of rainfall. Categories of drought remained unchanged by months end. Much of Collingsworth County remained in a 6 to 12 inch rainfall deficit year to date.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong upper level trough progressed through the Rockies and into the Central and Southern Plains during the day on November 4th, enhancing strong surface low development over the Upper Red River Valley into Oklahoma. This produced a strong pressure gradient over the Southern Plains and Lower Mississippi Valley, allowing for very rich Gulf moisture to surge north across the Ark-La-Tex area into Eastern Oklahoma and much of Arkansas. This generated moderate instability across these areas during the afternoon, as temperatures rose into the lower to mid 80s. Very strong wind shear was also in place over these areas, with the upper trough reinforcing a cold front southeast into Southeast Oklahoma, Western Arkansas, and East Texas. This trough enhanced large scale forcing along the front, with discrete supercell development also occurring ahead of the main line of storms over portions of East Texas, Southeast Oklahoma, and Southwest Arkansas. Multiple tornadoes, some strong, touched down across these areas, with additional instances of damaging winds also reported before the line of storms overtook these discrete supercells and shifted east across the remainder of East Texas, Southwest Arkansas, and into North Louisiana during the evening and overnight hours.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A damage survey team initially found damage east of Pittsburg in Camp County, Texas in association with a northeastward moving supercell thunderstorm which eventually went on to produce four tornadoes through northeast Texas and into southwest Arkansas. This initial EF-1 tornado with estimated maximum winds of 95 mph produced only minor tree damage, beginning near FM-2254 and traveling a few miles through rural areas before ending near CR-4244.

Some of these storms became severe, with reports of damaging winds across portions of East Texas during the morning hours.

A thunderstorm that developed over northwest Amarillo moved east and collided with a westward moving outflow boundary.  This caused the thunderstorm to intensify.  The storm produced golf ball size hail and half dollar size hail to the east of Amarillo.  Two outflow boundaries collided to the southeast of Amarillo causing a brief landspout.  A severe wind gust was recorded west of Lipscomb from an isolated severe storm.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level shortwave trough moved east-northeast through southeast Colorado and northeast New Mexico during the afternoon and evening hours.  Isolated severe thunderstorms developed in the southern and northeast Texas Panhandle.  Shear and instability were weak.  Thunderstorms were generally unorganized and formed in clusters.  A thunderstorm that developed over northwest Amarillo moved east and collided with a westward moving outflow boundary.  This caused the thunderstorm to intensify.  The storm produced golf ball size hail and half dollar size hail to the east of Amarillo.  Two outflow boundaries collided to the southeast of Amarillo causing a brief landspout.  A severe wind gust was recorded west of Lipscomb from an isolated severe storm.

A strong upper level trough progressed through the Rockies and into the Central and Southern Plains during the day on November 4th, enhancing strong surface low development over the Upper Red River Valley into Oklahoma. This produced a strong pressure gradient over the Southern Plains and Lower Mississippi Valley, allowing for very rich Gulf moisture to surge north across the Ark-La-Tex area into Eastern Oklahoma and much of Arkansas. This generated moderate instability across these areas during the afternoon, as temperatures rose into the lower to mid 80s. Very strong wind shear was also in place over these areas, with the upper trough reinforcing a cold front southeast into Southeast Oklahoma, Western Arkansas, and East Texas. This trough enhanced large scale forcing along the front, with discrete supercell development also occurring ahead of the main line of storms over portions of East Texas, Southeast Oklahoma, and Southwest Arkansas. Multiple tornadoes, some strong, touched down across these areas, with additional instances of damaging winds also reported before the line of storms overtook these discrete supercells and shifted east across the remainder of East Texas, Southwest Arkansas, and into North Louisiana during the evening and overnight hours.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An EF-4 tornado initially touched down near the Fulbright community southwest of Clarksville. An aerial survey confirmed that the tornado damage was to tin metal roof panels that were peeled off of a plant on CR-1200. As the tornado continued northeast, near FM-411, a single family home had all of its walls removed with only the interior room left standing where a family of three sheltered where winds were estimated at 150 mph. After it crossed FM-411, it hit another single family home and collapsed all the walls, injuring a woman who left her vehicle to take shelter inside the home. The tornado continued on to CR-1275 where debarking of a few trees was first observed in addition to thousands of trees that were snapped and uprooted throughout the path of the tornado. It then crossed US-82, CR-2123, CR-2124, and FM-2283. At FM-2283, it destroyed a single family home along with several outbuildings. This area could not be surveyed at this location as debris removal had already begun. The tornado then continued to move along CR-2125 and CR-2030 before taking a more eastward jog across SH-37. At this point, it is estimated that it was about a third of a mile wide and it began to widen further as it demonstrated more widespread tree snaps and isolated debarking throughout the remainder of Red River County. After crossing SH-37, the tornado wiped a single family home off of its foundation north of Clarksville with large portions of the walls and roof carried several hundred yards northeast of the home. This damage was surrounded by widespread tree snaps with isolated debarking. This location was reviewed by a regional Quick Response Team (QRT) that determined the damage at this location was EF-4 with maximum winds of 170 mph. This was based on the construction of the home, the debris field spread 50-200 yards downstream from the home in small pieces, and the slab of the home being wiped clean. Ten people on the property of the home took shelter in an oil drain of a metal outbuilding that was completely destroyed with no injuries. The damage swath widened to approximately 0.6 miles northeast of Clarksville as it approached Acworth and continued to cross the Red River. Before it crossed the Red River, it collapsed all the walls on a single family home and completely destroyed Mount Olive Church. It then lifted a double-wide manufactured home off the ground near FM-1159 and threw it 50 yards with three dogs inside that all survived. The tornado then crossed the Red River into south-central McCurtain County, Oklahoma.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A mid-level trough extended northeastward from northern Mexico through the Permian Basin. Enhanced atmospheric lift and rich low and mid-level moisture were across West Texas and Southeast New Mexico. These conditions contributed to heavy rain. This rain moved over saturated soils and resulted in flash flooding across parts of West Texas and Southeast New Mexico.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Heavy rain resulted in flooding in Big Bend National Park. All dirt roads, backcountry roadside campsites, and at least one paved road were closed throughout Big Bend National Park due to flooding. The cost of damage is a very rough estimate.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: By the middle of September, the long term drought improved to severe (D2) drought or better across the entire region. Showers and thunderstorms with heavy rain falling mainly in late August and early September helped rebound the annual rainfall deficit over the area with a good portion of the area showing much above normal rainfall. The rainfall was still less abundant over the extreme southern Texas Panhandle the southwestern South Plains. Most areas have seen rainfall greater than 150 percent of normal with some areas exceeding 300 percent of normal. The much needed rain brought relief to ranching operations where grasses and vegetation are finally starting to grow. In contrast, many farming operations including the vast number of acres dedicated to cotton, the rain came too late. The extreme drought over the summer caused a total failure or near total failure of the crops with limited or no irrigation. Overall yields of all crops for this year's growing season are expected to be down significantly from an average year.
